discovery.question: A candle burns inside a sealed glass jar sitting on a digital balance. The wax visibly shrinks and the flame dies — yet the reading never budges. What explains it?
options: Every product including the gases stayed trapped, so total mass is unchanged
The balance is too slow to register the loss before the flame dies
Burning converts mass into heat energy, which a balance cannot detect
The jar's glass absorbs the mass that the wax loses
discovery.answer: Every product including the gases stayed trapped, so total mass is unchanged
discovery.hook: Mass isn't destroyed when matter transforms — it only looks destroyed when gases escape the account.

c11_chem_ch01.mission: Run a chemical audit of a schoolbag — name the designed molecule behind everyday items — then verify mass conservation in a sealed reaction.
c11_chem_ch01.finale: Chemistry doesn't just explain matter, it designs it — and its first law is that nothing is ever truly lost.
c11_chem_ch01.subtitle: See why chemistry is called the central science, and why a sealed system never loses mass.
c11_chem_ch01.role: a materials analyst tracing the chemistry hidden in everyday objects
c11_chem_ch01.intro: A shopkeeper swears rusting, ripening and burning are 'just things that happen.' You're here to show the molecular machinery underneath.
c11_chem_ch01.goal: Recognise chemistry's reach across daily life and apply conservation of mass to closed systems.

discovery.question: In Thomson's tube, an electron beam passes straight when electric and magnetic fields are tuned to cancel. Switch off the electric field and the beam curves into a circle. What does the circle's radius let you measure?
options: The electron's charge-to-mass ratio
The electron's exact charge
The electron's exact mass
The speed of light inside the tube
discovery.answer: The electron's charge-to-mass ratio
discovery.hook: Fields can only weigh charge against mass together — the ratio falls out, never either quantity alone.

c11_chem_ch02.mission: Balance crossed fields to read off beam speed, then extract e/m from the radius of the circle the beam carves.
c11_chem_ch02.finale: Thomson couldn't see an electron — so he bent it, balanced it, and measured the ratio that made it universal.
c11_chem_ch02.subtitle: See how crossed fields proved cathode rays are particles and pinned down e/m.
c11_chem_ch02.role: a physicist reproducing Thomson's cathode-ray measurements
c11_chem_ch02.intro: A glowing beam in a vacuum tube — light or matter? Your fields will decide.
c11_chem_ch02.goal: Explain why field deflection proves particle nature and how crossed fields yield the charge-to-mass ratio.

discovery.question: Mendeleev placed tellurium (heavier) before iodine (lighter), breaking his own atomic-weight rule. What justified the swap?
options: Their chemical properties demanded those group positions
He made a measurement error that was quietly corrected later
Tellurium had originally been assigned the wrong symbol
Heavier elements were always placed later no matter what
discovery.answer: Their chemical properties demanded those group positions
discovery.hook: Mendeleev trusted properties over his own rule — Moseley's X-rays later proved atomic number was the real ordering all along.

c11_chem_ch03.mission: Slot four unknown elements into a Mendeleev-style group, predict a missing element's chloride formula, then place element 35 in the modern table.
c11_chem_ch03.finale: The periodic table works because electron configurations repeat — atomic number just made the pattern honest.
c11_chem_ch03.subtitle: Test why properties outrank mass, and how atomic number fixed the table's anomalies.
c11_chem_ch03.role: a chemist stress-testing the periodic table's logic
c11_chem_ch03.intro: A drawer of unlabelled reagent bottles and a table with gaps — your job is to make order defend itself.
c11_chem_ch03.goal: Distinguish atomic-weight ordering from the modern atomic-number law and use both to place elements.

discovery.question: Making Na+ from Na costs +496 kJ/mol and making Cl- releases only -349 kJ/mol — the gas-phase ions are still +147 kJ/mol in the red, yet salt forms spontaneously. What pays the bill?
options: The huge lattice enthalpy released when gaseous ions pack into a crystal
The octet rule makes the energy debt disappear
Chlorine donates the missing energy back to sodium
Room temperature automatically supplies the deficit
discovery.answer: The huge lattice enthalpy released when gaseous ions pack into a crystal
discovery.hook: Completing octets isn't what makes ionic solids stable — the pay-off is in the packing, about -788 kJ/mol for NaCl.

c11_chem_ch04.mission: Build a Born-Haber energy ledger for NaCl and decide whether octet completion or lattice enthalpy really drives its formation.
c11_chem_ch04.finale: Ionic bonds aren't paid for by octets — they're paid for when countless ions snap into a lattice.
c11_chem_ch04.subtitle: Weigh electron bookkeeping against lattice energy to explain why salt exists at all.
c11_chem_ch04.role: an energeticist auditing why ionic crystals form
c11_chem_ch04.intro: Sodium and chlorine both 'want' noble-gas shells — but the energy ledger is still in the red. Find who foots the bill.
c11_chem_ch04.goal: Apply Kossel-Lewis electron accounting and use Born-Haber energetics to explain ionic bond formation.

discovery.question: Nonpolar iodine (I2) boils at 184°C while polar HCl boils at -85°C. If dipole-dipole forces always beat London forces, this is backwards. What actually decides it?
options: I2's large polarizable electron cloud gives London forces that outweigh HCl's dipole forces
HCl's dipole is too weak to matter at any temperature
Iodine secretly hydrogen-bonds like water does
Molar mass directly sets boiling point regardless of forces
discovery.answer: I2's large polarizable electron cloud gives London forces that outweigh HCl's dipole forces
discovery.hook: Every molecule has London forces — a permanent dipole is a bonus on top, and a big electron cloud can outmuscle polarity.

c11_chem_ch05.mission: Rank the Group 14 hydrides by boiling point using polarizability, then explain why nonpolar I2 outboils polar HCl.
c11_chem_ch05.finale: Intermolecular attraction isn't a loyalty test — the biggest, most distortable electron cloud usually wins.
c11_chem_ch05.subtitle: Separate London, dipole-dipole and hydrogen-bond contributions and predict who boils first.
c11_chem_ch05.role: a physical chemist explaining anomalous boiling points
c11_chem_ch05.intro: A gecko walks up glass and iodine leaps straight to vapour — name the invisible grip behind both.
c11_chem_ch05.goal: Distinguish London dispersion from dipole-dipole forces and use polarizability to predict boiling trends.

discovery.question: A sealed pressure cooker sits on a flame — no steam escapes, but heat pours in. A student calls it an isolated system and sets q = 0. What is it really?
options: A closed system — matter is fixed but heat still crosses the boundary
An isolated system — nothing material leaves, so nothing counts as exchanged
An open system — the steam inside is still moving
Closed and isolated mean the same thing here
discovery.answer: A closed system — matter is fixed but heat still crosses the boundary
discovery.hook: 'Closed' seals matter, not energy — confusing the two silently wrecks every first-law sign that follows.

c11_chem_ch06.mission: Classify a pressure cooker, a thermos flask and an open beaker, then run a P-V cycle to show work is path-dependent while internal energy returns to zero.
c11_chem_ch06.finale: Pick the boundary honestly and the first law is clean bookkeeping; pick it wrong and every sign flips.
c11_chem_ch06.subtitle: Draw the system boundary correctly and track energy as heat and work.
c11_chem_ch06.role: a thermodynamic accountant auditing a steam system
c11_chem_ch06.intro: Same cooker, three seal states — each changes what energy is allowed to cross your ledger.
c11_chem_ch06.goal: Classify open, closed and isolated systems and apply the first law with correct sign conventions.

discovery.question: Radioactive sugar crystals dropped into a saturated solution soon make the liquid radioactive — while the amount dissolved stays constant. What does that prove?
options: Dissolving and crystallising continue at equal rates — equilibrium is dynamic, not frozen
Radioactivity forces extra sugar to dissolve
The solution was never truly saturated
Crystals only dissolve when the solution is disturbed
discovery.answer: Dissolving and crystallising continue at equal rates — equilibrium is dynamic, not frozen
discovery.hook: Equal rates, not equal amounts — at equilibrium the molecular exchange never stops; the totals just quit changing.

c11_chem_ch07.mission: Track concentrations in H2 + I2 ⇌ 2HI until they plateau, then test what adding more H2 does to NH3 yield versus the equilibrium constant.
c11_chem_ch07.finale: Equilibrium is a busy standstill — shove the position all you like; only temperature moves the constant.
c11_chem_ch07.subtitle: See why equilibrium means equal rates — and why Kc ignores concentration shoves.
c11_chem_ch07.role: a reaction engineer steering a reversible process
c11_chem_ch07.intro: The reaction looks finished; the molecules disagree. Prove the traffic still runs both ways.
c11_chem_ch07.goal: Describe dynamic equilibrium and distinguish the equilibrium position from the equilibrium constant.

discovery.question: Hydrogen burns in chlorine — H2 + Cl2 → 2HCl — with no oxygen anywhere in sight. Is anything being oxidised?
options: Yes — hydrogen loses electrons to chlorine; oxidation needs no oxygen
No — oxidation requires oxygen by definition
Only chlorine is oxidised, since it gains the hydrogen
Neither — this is just a combination reaction
discovery.answer: Yes — hydrogen loses electrons to chlorine; oxidation needs no oxygen
discovery.hook: Oxygen lent its name to oxidation, but electron loss is the real event — no O2 required.

c11_chem_ch08.mission: Assign oxidation numbers across sulfur's compounds and explain why the two nitrogens in NH4NO3 carry different oxidation states.
c11_chem_ch08.finale: Oxidation numbers are bookkeeping, not real charges — but they catch every electron that changes hands.
c11_chem_ch08.subtitle: Track electrons with oxidation numbers even where oxygen never appears.
c11_chem_ch08.role: a redox auditor tracing electron transfers
c11_chem_ch08.intro: A nail rusts and a copper wire grows a coat of silver — count who lost electrons and who collected them.
c11_chem_ch08.goal: Define oxidation and reduction beyond oxygen and assign oxidation numbers correctly.

discovery.question: Hydrogen forms H+ like an alkali metal, yet its ionisation enthalpy (1312 kJ/mol) sits near fluorine's, far above lithium's 520. Where does it belong in the periodic table?
options: Apart — it borrows one feature from Group 1 and another from Group 17 but fits neither
Group 1 — forming H+ settles it
Group 17 — the high ionisation enthalpy settles it
Group 14 — because it is a gas like no metal
discovery.answer: Apart — it borrows one feature from Group 1 and another from Group 17 but fits neither
discovery.hook: A bare proton is no stable cation like Na+ — it has no electron cloud and must hitchhike on water as H3O+.

c11_chem_ch09.mission: Pit hydrogen's ionisation and electron-gain data against lithium and fluorine, then separate how protium, deuterium and tritium actually behave.
c11_chem_ch09.finale: Hydrogen is the periodic table's orphan — one electron, two borrowed identities, no true home group.
c11_chem_ch09.subtitle: Judge hydrogen's split personality and what really separates its three isotopes.
c11_chem_ch09.role: a classification referee deciding hydrogen's address
c11_chem_ch09.intro: Every group claims hydrogen for one property and rejects it for another — hear the evidence and rule.
c11_chem_ch09.goal: Evaluate hydrogen's resemblance to Groups 1 and 17 and distinguish the properties of its isotopes.

discovery.question: An abacus, Pascal's Pascaline and Babbage's Analytical Engine all perform calculations. Only one is a true ancestor of the computer — which, and what's the dividing line?
options: The Analytical Engine — it was programmable via punched cards, with input, store, mill and output
The abacus — it is the oldest, so everything descends from it
The Pascaline — gears make it a real machine, unlike the others
All three — calculation alone makes a device a computer
discovery.answer: The Analytical Engine — it was programmable via punched cards, with input, store, mill and output
discovery.hook: Calculating isn't computing — the line is programmability: stored instructions driving automatic execution.

c11_cs_ch01.mission: Sort a school's attendance data into structured, unstructured and semi-structured, then separate the hardware from the software that boots a laptop.
c11_cs_ch01.finale: A computer isn't a clever calculator — it's a machine that runs stored instructions on whatever data you feed it.
c11_cs_ch01.subtitle: Draw the line between calculators and computers, and between memory and storage.
c11_cs_ch01.role: a systems archivist sorting devices and data formats
c11_cs_ch01.intro: A museum labels every calculating gadget a 'computer.' Your job is to correct the record.
c11_cs_ch01.goal: Identify the components of a computer system and classify data and software correctly.

discovery.question: A logic expression reads 1 + 1. Arithmetic says 2, binary says 10 — what does a digital circuit say, and why?
options: 1 — in Boolean algebra '+' means OR, and true-OR-true is true
10 — circuits work in binary so it must carry
2 — the symbol keeps its arithmetic meaning everywhere
0 — two identical inputs cancel out
discovery.answer: 1 — in Boolean algebra '+' means OR, and true-OR-true is true
discovery.hook: Same symbol, different algebra — in logic, '+' is a doorway (OR), not a sum.

c11_cs_ch02.mission: Build truth tables for a smart light that needs motion AND night, and a phone that unlocks with fingerprint OR PIN.
c11_cs_ch02.finale: Every decision a computer makes — from alarms to unlock screens — is just two-state variables and three little operations.
c11_cs_ch02.subtitle: Map real-world and/or decisions onto Boolean variables that only know 0 and 1.
c11_cs_ch02.role: a logic designer wiring a home security rule
c11_cs_ch02.intro: An alarm should fire only if the door opens AND the system is armed — turn that sentence into algebra.
c11_cs_ch02.goal: Represent two-state conditions as Boolean variables and combine them with AND, OR and NOT.

discovery.question: A student codes a kirana bill — 10% discount above ₹500, then 5% GST — and the code runs. Yet the bill is wrong. What did skipping the analysis step hide?
options: Whether GST applies to the original total or the discounted total was never decided
Python cannot compute percentages without a library
The discount should legally be applied after GST
input() always returns numbers, so no checking was needed
discovery.answer: Whether GST applies to the original total or the discounted total was never decided
discovery.hook: Code is a translation — the ambiguity that breaks it was born upstream, in the analysis nobody did.

c11_cs_ch03.mission: Draw the full IPO table for a canteen bill — inputs with data types, a conditional discount, a formatted output — then test the boundary values 499, 500 and 501.
c11_cs_ch03.finale: Solve on paper first; the algorithm that survives a flowchart rarely dies in an editor.
c11_cs_ch03.subtitle: Analyse before you code: inputs, process and output, pinned down to data types.
c11_cs_ch03.role: a junior developer scoping a shop-billing app
c11_cs_ch03.intro: The shopkeeper wants a billing app by Friday. The fastest route starts with a pen, not a keyboard.
c11_cs_ch03.goal: Break a problem into input-process-output and design a testable algorithm before coding.

discovery.question: A student types a 20-line program into the >>> shell, closes the window and loses everything. What did they confuse?
options: The interactive shell, which runs lines and forgets them, with the editor that saves scripts
Python with the operating system's notepad
The interpreter with the compiler — the code needed compiling first
Save with run — F5 saves files automatically
discovery.answer: The interactive shell, which runs lines and forgets them, with the editor that saves scripts
discovery.hook: The >>> prompt is a conversation, not a document — scripts live in files, and files need saving.

c11_cs_ch04.mission: Install Python, recover from a forgotten 'Add to PATH' checkbox, then write and run a cost.py script from IDLE's editor.
c11_cs_ch04.finale: Python trades raw speed for speed of thought — you can fix and re-run a line faster than most languages compile.
c11_cs_ch04.subtitle: Get Python running, know shell from editor, and see why interpreted means instant feedback.
c11_cs_ch04.role: a developer setting up a first Python workspace
c11_cs_ch04.intro: The installer finished, but `python` 'is not recognized.' Diagnose the machine before writing a line.
c11_cs_ch04.goal: Set up Python and IDLE, distinguish the interactive shell from script mode, and run a first program.

discovery.question: Halfway through a while loop's body, a variable makes the condition false. Does the loop bail out instantly?
options: No — the condition is only checked at the top; the current iteration finishes first
Yes — Python watches the condition like a sensor
Yes — but only for numeric conditions
No — a while loop never stops once started
discovery.answer: No — the condition is only checked at the top; the current iteration finishes first
discovery.hook: The condition is a gate at the top of the loop, not a tripwire inside it — mid-body changes wait their turn.

c11_cs_ch05.mission: Write a countdown loop from 10 to 2, build the even-number sum two ways, then predict what Python does with "10" > 2.
c11_cs_ch05.finale: Selection chooses a path once; iteration walks it again and again — and only ever checks at the door.
c11_cs_ch05.subtitle: Control the flow: conditions that decide and loops that repeat, without lying about when they check.
c11_cs_ch05.role: a programmer automating a rickshaw fare table
c11_cs_ch05.intro: One fixed distance, one formula — useless. Real riders go 2 km or 20 km, and your code must bend.
c11_cs_ch05.goal: Use if/elif/else, while and for to make programs decide and repeat correctly.

discovery.question: name = "Aarav" works, and name[0] reads 'A' fine — but name[0] = "K" to make 'Karav' throws TypeError. What rule did the assignment break?
options: Strings are immutable — 'edits' must build a new string, never rewrite in place
Index 0 is reserved and cannot be assigned to
Single characters can't be stored in variables
The string was created with double quotes, which lock it
discovery.answer: Strings are immutable — 'edits' must build a new string, never rewrite in place
discovery.hook: Indexing reads fine — writing is what's banned. Immutability means every 'change' is actually a fresh string.

c11_cs_ch06.mission: Extract 'CBSE' and '2025' from the ID 'CBSE2025', grab the last character without hardcoding an index, and store a sentence containing both quote types.
c11_cs_ch06.finale: A string is an ordered row of characters you can read from either end — but never rewrite in place.
c11_cs_ch06.subtitle: Index from zero, slice out substrings, and learn why strings refuse in-place edits.
c11_cs_ch06.role: a data clerk carving fields out of text records
c11_cs_ch06.intro: Forms want pieces of an ID card — board here, year there. Your scalpel is the index.
c11_cs_ch06.goal: Use zero-based indexing and slicing on strings and explain string immutability.

discovery.question: You write t = (5) expecting a one-item tuple — but type(t) says int. What actually makes a tuple?
options: The comma — (5,) is a tuple; parentheses only group
The parentheses — but only with two or more items
The tuple() constructor — nothing else counts
Square brackets are required for single items
discovery.answer: The comma — (5,) is a tuple; parentheses only group
discovery.hook: Parentheses are decoration; the comma is the signature. Even t = 1, 2, 3 is a tuple.

c11_cs_ch07.mission: Store the RGB triple (255, 153, 51), slice out (30, 40) using negative indices, then argue tuple over list for twelve fixed monthly targets.
c11_cs_ch07.finale: A tuple is a sealed envelope — read anything inside, change nothing, and let the seal itself signal 'fixed.'
c11_cs_ch07.subtitle: Use tuples for data that must not move — and learn that it's the comma, not the bracket, that seals it.
c11_cs_ch07.role: a developer guarding data that must stay constant
c11_cs_ch07.intro: Twelve sales targets, fixed all year. Choose a container that makes 'unchangeable' a feature, not a hope.
c11_cs_ch07.goal: Create, index and slice tuples and justify immutability as a design choice.

discovery.question: A module loads, reaching a def block that contains a print — yet nothing appears on screen. Is the code broken?
options: No — def only stores the recipe; nothing inside runs until the function is called
Yes — print inside a function always runs at load
No — but only because print is ignored inside functions
Yes — the colon after the parameter list was missing
discovery.answer: No — def only stores the recipe; nothing inside runs until the function is called
discovery.hook: Definition is a stored recipe, not a cooked meal — Python reads the def, shelves it, and waits for a call.

c11_cs_ch08.mission: Write calculate_fine(days_late, rate) for a library, then give two teammates a shared book_exists() helper instead of duplicated checks.
c11_cs_ch08.finale: Functions aren't just copy-paste insurance — they're named decisions you can call, test and fix in one place.
c11_cs_ch08.subtitle: Package logic into named, reusable blocks — and learn why defining runs nothing.
c11_cs_ch08.role: a programmer modularising a library system
c11_cs_ch08.intro: Three teammates, three features, one duplicated check. Refactor it into a function they can all call.
c11_cs_ch08.goal: Define and call functions with parameters, and explain reusability and maintainability.

discovery.question: Rename photo.jpg to photo.txt and open it in Notepad — gibberish. Did the file become a text file?
options: No — the internal byte structure defines the type; the extension is only a hint
Yes — the .txt extension converts the contents automatically
Yes — but only after Notepad finishes reading it
No — because .jpg files cannot be renamed
discovery.answer: No — the internal byte structure defines the type; the extension is only a hint
discovery.hook: An extension is a label on the box, not a conversion of what's inside — bytes decide the file type.

c11_cs_ch09.mission: Open records/data.csv for reading, pick the right mode to write a JPEG without corruption, and choose a human-readable format for student records.
c11_cs_ch09.finale: open() doesn't read anything — it hands you a handle; what flows through depends on the mode you chose.
c11_cs_ch09.subtitle: Persist data beyond the program — and never trust an extension to tell you a file's type.
c11_cs_ch09.role: a developer building a contact-saver app
c11_cs_ch09.intro: Marks for 500 students vanish when the program exits. Files are how data outlives the run.
c11_cs_ch09.goal: Distinguish text from binary files and use open() with the correct mode and path.

discovery.question: You implement a stack as a Python list: push with insert(0, x), pop with pop(0). It behaves correctly — so is it a real stack?
options: Only in behaviour — front operations shift every element, breaking the stack's O(1) contract
Yes — any list automatically qualifies as a stack
No — stacks are impossible to build in Python
Yes — because pop(0) removes the correct element
discovery.answer: Only in behaviour — front operations shift every element, breaking the stack's O(1) contract
discovery.hook: A data structure is a contract, not just a container — stacks promise constant-time ends, and a list's front can't keep that promise.

c11_cs_ch10.mission: Trace push(10), push(20), push(30), pop(), push(40), pop(), pop() step by step, then pick the right structure for the principal's waiting line.
c11_cs_ch10.finale: LIFO for undo and calls, FIFO for waiting lines — the restriction is the feature.
c11_cs_ch10.subtitle: Choose between stack and queue by asking who gets served first.
c11_cs_ch10.role: a programmer choosing structures for a playlist app
c11_cs_ch10.intro: Newest song first or first-come first-served? The access pattern picks the structure, not the other way round.
c11_cs_ch10.goal: Model LIFO and FIFO behaviour and justify why restricted access is an advantage.

discovery.question: A school lab's computers share files and one printer, but the internet is down. Is the lab still a network?
options: Yes — a LAN exists on its own; the internet is a service that rides on networks, not a requirement
No — without internet there is nothing to share
Only if the computers use cables, since Wi-Fi needs internet
No — a network requires a server connected to the web
discovery.answer: Yes — a LAN exists on its own; the internet is a service that rides on networks, not a requirement
discovery.hook: Network ≠ internet — two machines sharing a printer are already a network; the web is just the biggest one.

c11_cs_ch11.mission: Map sender, receiver, medium and protocol for phone-to-printer and laptop-to-TV, then classify a campus network versus a city-spanning link.
c11_cs_ch11.finale: Geography and ownership classify a network — LAN for a campus, MAN for a city — not the cable or the speed.
c11_cs_ch11.subtitle: See what makes devices a network and why LAN, MAN and WAN are measured in geography, not wires.
c11_cs_ch11.role: an IT planner connecting a school's devices
c11_cs_ch11.intro: Four devices, one printer, one movie — figure out who talks to whom, over what medium, speaking which protocol.
c11_cs_ch11.goal: Identify network components and classify networks by geographical span.

discovery.question: The British left India the world's fourth-largest railway network — often cited as proof colonial rule modernised the economy. What does the network's design reveal?
options: Port-to-hinterland lines built to move raw materials out, at a guaranteed 5% return paid from Indian revenues
Inter-regional lines designed to integrate Indian markets for Indian industry
Routes chosen to connect famine-prone districts to food surpluses
A passenger-first network funded by British taxpayers
discovery.answer: Port-to-hinterland lines built to move raw materials out, at a guaranteed 5% return paid from Indian revenues
discovery.hook: Infrastructure isn't automatically development — ask who paid for it, who profited, and what it was built to carry.

c11_eco_ch01.mission: Weigh the social benefits of railways and telegraphs against surplus extraction, then show how population growth erased per-capita gains.
c11_eco_ch01.finale: Colonialism didn't leave India without activity — it left activity wired to serve someone else's economy.
c11_eco_ch01.subtitle: Separate real infrastructure from developmental impact on the eve of independence.
c11_eco_ch01.role: an economic historian auditing two centuries of colonial policy
c11_eco_ch01.intro: A weaver's looms in 1750 Bengal stand idle by 1850 while Lancashire hums. Trace the policy that flipped the trade.
c11_eco_ch01.goal: Explain colonial exploitation, deindustrialisation and per-capita stagnation under British rule.

discovery.question: The First Five Year Plan poured 44.6% of its outlay into agriculture and irrigation. Critics called it backward-looking next to the Second Plan's steel plants. What was the real logic?
options: A model-based choice: food was the binding constraint and irrigation gave fast returns on little capital
Tradition — planners simply had no industrial model available
Foreign pressure forced food-first spending
Agriculture was already the most modern sector
discovery.answer: A model-based choice: food was the binding constraint and irrigation gave fast returns on little capital
discovery.hook: Self-reliance never meant 'import nothing' — it meant not importing what India could produce; food still came in under PL-480.

c11_eco_ch02.mission: Apply compound growth to First-Plan GDP, then test whether self-reliance banned imports or only needless ones.
c11_eco_ch02.finale: Planning is rationing ambition — the early plans spent scarcest resources on the constraint that would have strangled everything else.
c11_eco_ch02.subtitle: Weigh the four goals of planning and the agriculture-first bet of 1951.
c11_eco_ch02.intro: 360 million people, food grain at 51 million tonnes, the Bengal famine eight years behind you. Spend the plan.
c11_eco_ch02.goal: Explain the goals of Five Year Plans and justify the First Plan's agricultural priority.

discovery.question: In July 1991 the rupee was devalued 18-19%, and many accounts call that the moment the crisis 'began.' What does the timeline actually show?
options: Devaluation was the corrective response — reserves had already collapsed to roughly two weeks of imports
Devaluation caused the crisis by shrinking reserves overnight
The crisis was invented to justify an IMF loan
Reserves were healthy; only the fiscal deficit triggered reform
discovery.answer: Devaluation was the corrective response — reserves had already collapsed to roughly two weeks of imports
discovery.hook: Cause and cure get confused when they sit a week apart — the devaluation was medicine for a decade of deficits, not the disease.

c11_eco_ch03.mission: Compute import cover from reserves and monthly imports, then separate liberalisation from privatisation in the LPG package.
c11_eco_ch03.finale: 1991 wasn't a choice to open up — it was a bill coming due, and the conditions rewired how India produces and trades.
c11_eco_ch03.subtitle: Follow the 1991 crisis from drained reserves to the LPG reforms it forced.
c11_eco_ch03.role: a policy analyst dissecting the 1991 bailout
c11_eco_ch03.intro: A household spending ₹70,000 on ₹50,000 income eventually meets a lender with conditions. In 1991, that household was India.
c11_eco_ch03.goal: Explain the balance-of-payments crisis and distinguish liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation.

discovery.question: One father owns a ₹50 lakh loom; another holds a ₹20 lakh engineering degree. Which capital can be sold without its owner showing up?
options: The loom — human capital is embodied in the person and cannot be transferred separately
The degree — certificates can be sold to the highest bidder
Both — capital is capital regardless of form
Neither — once bought, capital is locked to its owner
discovery.answer: The loom — human capital is embodied in the person and cannot be transferred separately
discovery.hook: The engineer isn't the capital — the skills are. And unlike the loom, they can't be leased out or shipped abroad.

c11_eco_ch04.mission: Compare a machine's depreciation against an operator's rising productivity, then price a family's migration as an investment with a payback period.
c11_eco_ch04.finale: Human capital is spent into people — and because its benefits spill over to society, leaving it to private wallets alone underfunds it.
c11_eco_ch04.subtitle: Distinguish embodied skill from sellable machines, and investment flow from capital stock.
c11_eco_ch04.role: an economist pricing investments in people
c11_eco_ch04.intro: ₹50,000: a tractor or a nursing diploma? Both are bets on future returns — but only one walks away on its own feet.
c11_eco_ch04.goal: Define human capital, contrast it with physical capital, and identify its sources of formation.

discovery.question: A Maharashtra village: 70% of households farm, 15% have institutional credit, the nearest cold storage is 40 km away — while India's GDP grows 7%. Why is the village stuck?
options: A structural mismatch — about 42% of the workforce produces only 15% of GDP
Villagers refuse to adopt new farming techniques
Rural poverty is just what happens before cities develop
Credit is available; farmers simply choose not to borrow
discovery.answer: A structural mismatch — about 42% of the workforce produces only 15% of GDP
discovery.hook: Rural development isn't charity or more roads — it's fixing a workforce trapped where productivity is lowest.

c11_eco_ch05.mission: Compute farm versus non-farm output per worker, then test whether more bank branches or Jan-Dhan accounts equal real credit access.
c11_eco_ch05.finale: Access isn't adequacy — an account that can't lend and a bank that demands land as collateral both leave the moneylender in business.
c11_eco_ch05.subtitle: Diagnose why villages lag a booming GDP — credit, productivity and missing non-farm links.
c11_eco_ch05.role: a rural development officer auditing a district
c11_eco_ch05.intro: The sowing is in June, the payment in October — four months of costs, and the moneylender charges 5% a month.
c11_eco_ch05.goal: Explain rural development as structural correction and analyse the rural credit gap.

discovery.question: A graduate registers at an employment exchange and is still searching. Is she in the workforce?
options: No — she's in the labour force, which is workforce plus those seeking work
Yes — registering makes her a worker by definition
Yes — she counts toward the worker-population ratio
No — she is economically inactive until hired
discovery.answer: No — she's in the labour force, which is workforce plus those seeking work
discovery.hook: Labour force = workforce + seekers — swap them and both the WPR and the unemployment rate come out wrong.

c11_eco_ch06.mission: Compute a village's worker-population ratio and female casual share, then argue whether unpaid home work belongs in national income.
c11_eco_ch06.finale: Officially, work counts when it enters the market — which is why a breakfast cooked at home vanishes from GNP while the same meal at a stall doesn't.
c11_eco_ch06.subtitle: Sort workers from seekers and ask who the statistics leave out.
c11_eco_ch06.role: a labour statistician classifying a busy chowk
c11_eco_ch06.intro: Vendor, clerk, daily-wage painter, unpaid homemaker — decide which of them the national accounts can see.
c11_eco_ch06.goal: Distinguish labour force from workforce and classify employment types correctly.

discovery.question: Punjab's aquifers refill every monsoon — groundwater is renewable, so it can never run out. True?
options: False — tubewells extract roughly 35 BCM a year against about 21 BCM of recharge, making it non-renewable in practice
True — anything the rain replaces is by definition renewable
False — groundwater was never renewable
True — only coal and ores can be exhausted
discovery.answer: False — tubewells extract roughly 35 BCM a year against about 21 BCM of recharge, making it non-renewable in practice
discovery.hook: Renewable is a rate, not a category — extract faster than nature regenerates and 'renewable' is just a label.

c11_eco_ch07.mission: Classify six resources as renewable or not under real extraction rates, then price the nutrients India's eroding soil loses each year.
c11_eco_ch07.finale: The environment is a supplier, a sink and a life-support at once — degrade it and the bill lands on health, output and the next generation.
c11_eco_ch07.subtitle: Test what 'renewable' really means and cost the land India is losing.
c11_eco_ch07.role: an environmental auditor reading a farm's white crust
c11_eco_ch07.intro: A Punjab farmer finds salt crusting his fields after decades of canal irrigation. Trace how affluence and poverty each degrade the same land.
c11_eco_ch07.goal: Classify resources by regeneration rate and analyse the drivers and costs of land degradation.

discovery.question: China outlives and out-educates India on every human development table. A common story credits the 1978 market reforms. What does the timing show?
options: The gains were built pre-1978 — commune health schemes, barefoot doctors and universal primary schooling created the capacity reforms later exploited
Correct — markets alone produced the health and literacy lead
China's lead is just statistical inflation
India actually matches China once income is adjusted
discovery.answer: The gains were built pre-1978 — commune health schemes, barefoot doctors and universal primary schooling created the capacity reforms later exploited
discovery.hook: Reforms released growth; they didn't build the capacity — that was decades of health, schooling and land equity laid earlier.

c11_eco_ch08.mission: Use the rule of 70 on Pakistan's 1.96% population growth versus China's -0.10%, then separate what pre- and post-reform China each contributed.
c11_eco_ch08.finale: Three neighbours, one starting line — the scoreboard at 2020 was written by choices made decades apart.
c11_eco_ch08.subtitle: Read the India-Pakistan-China comparison as a contest of strategies, not just growth rates.
c11_eco_ch08.role: a development economist comparing three cousins' trajectories
c11_eco_ch08.intro: Same start line around 1950, three different scorecards. Ask which policies aged well — and which aged fast.
c11_eco_ch08.goal: Compare the development strategies and outcomes of India, China and Pakistan.

discovery.question: The narrator's grandmother declares music 'the monopoly of harlots and beggars.' Is this just one old woman's prejudice?
options: No — it encodes a broader class attitude of her era, when professional musicians came from communities respectable families shunned
Yes — a purely personal quirk with no cultural basis
No — she objected because music distracted from prayer, nothing more
Yes — she simply disliked the instrument the boy played
discovery.answer: No — it encodes a broader class attitude of her era, when professional musicians came from communities respectable families shunned
discovery.hook: She isn't 'backward' — she's a representative figure of a vanishing world, and her silences carry a whole generation's rules.

c11_eng_h_ch01.mission: Split the narrative into its three phases of companionship, separation and loss — then defend why the story ends with silent sparrows, not a funeral.
c11_eng_h_ch01.finale: The sparrows refusing their crumbs say what the family couldn't — her world mourned her in its own tongue.
c11_eng_h_ch01.subtitle: Read the grandmother as a vanishing world, not a quirky old woman.
c11_eng_h_ch01.role: a reader tracing a relationship across two Indias
c11_eng_h_ch01.intro: Village temple school to English city classroom — watch a bond dissolve not in anger but in syllabi.
c11_eng_h_ch01.goal: Use context and narrative phases to interpret the grandmother's values and the story's ending.

discovery.question: Fifteen hours of pumping and repairs fill most of the survival account — so is that the climax?
options: No — the climax is the single moment the wave strikes; the pumping is falling action after the peak
Yes — the longest, most dangerous stretch is always the climax
No — the climax is reaching the island safely
Yes — duration and effort define dramatic peak
discovery.answer: No — the climax is the single moment the wave strikes; the pumping is falling action after the peak
discovery.hook: Duration isn't intensity — the climax is the instant death became possible, not the long labour of surviving it.

c11_eng_h_ch02.mission: Map the three sections onto the five dramatic stages, then explain why the children's courage is saved for the falling action.
c11_eng_h_ch02.finale: Placing 'we aren't afraid of dying if we can all be together' after the wave turns a disaster log into a testament to family unity.
c11_eng_h_ch02.subtitle: Find the real climax of a survival story — and why the bravest line comes after it.
c11_eng_h_ch02.role: a narrator reconstructing a voyage that nearly killed everyone
c11_eng_h_ch02.intro: A businessman's family sets out to retrace Captain Cook's wake — and the Southern Ocean takes the dare.
c11_eng_h_ch02.goal: Analyse the narrative structure of a survival account and place its true climax.

discovery.question: The article opens on the 2005 CT scan, jumps back to Carter's 1922 dig, then further back to Akhenaten's reign. Why scramble the timeline?
options: The flashbacks are rising action — they build the mystery of Tut's death that the scan must solve
Chronology doesn't matter in non-fiction
The scan is dull, so history is added for colour
The author couldn't decide where to begin
discovery.answer: The flashbacks are rising action — they build the mystery of Tut's death that the scan must solve
discovery.hook: This is a cold case, not a chronicle — every jump backward is a clue the 2005 scan was called in to read.

c11_eng_h_ch03.mission: Reorder the article's events into narrative order versus historical order, then assess what Carter's chiselling did to the evidence modern forensics inherited.
c11_eng_h_ch03.finale: Tut's body reached the scanner already broken — by the resins that buried him and the rescue that dismembered him.
c11_eng_h_ch03.subtitle: Read a 3,300-year-old cold case where the first detectives damaged the body.
c11_eng_h_ch03.role: a forensic reader working a pharaoh's cold case
c11_eng_h_ch03.intro: A mummy cemented in gold by ritual resins, a scan three millennia late — reconstruct what each era did to the evidence.
c11_eng_h_ch03.goal: Distinguish narrative order from chronology and evaluate how earlier interventions shaped the forensic record.

discovery.question: A common verdict: Chinese landscape painting looks 'less realistic' because its painters never mastered perspective. What's wrong with that?
options: They knew perspective but rejected it — the goal was conceptual completeness across viewpoints, not one frozen optical illusion
Nothing — they genuinely lacked the technique until Europe arrived
They avoided perspective only because paper scrolls were too small
Realism was banned under imperial decree
discovery.answer: They knew perspective but rejected it — the goal was conceptual completeness across viewpoints, not one frozen optical illusion
discovery.hook: Judging Shanshui by European realism is a rigged test — the European painter lends you his eyes; the Chinese painter invites you into his mind.

c11_eng_h_ch04.mission: Contrast single-viewpoint perspective with a scroll's travelling viewpoints, then test whether 'landscape of the soul' implies a greener relationship to nature.
c11_eng_h_ch04.finale: A European landscape is a window you look through; a Chinese one is a country you wander — the difference is a philosophy, not a skill gap.
c11_eng_h_ch04.subtitle: See why Chinese painters walked away from the single fixed viewpoint on purpose.
c11_eng_h_ch04.role: a curator comparing two wings of an art museum
c11_eng_h_ch04.intro: Misty mountains with tiny humans on one side, pin-sharp portraits on the other — decide what each culture was really painting.
c11_eng_h_ch04.goal: Contrast the Chinese and European landscape traditions and interpret 'landscape of the soul.'

discovery.question: A student writes: 'The Green Movement increased wheat yields in Punjab.' What went wrong?
options: They merged two different things — the Green Movement is the post-1972 environmental conscience; the Green Revolution was the 1960s farm technology
Nothing — the movement directly raised yields
The yields rose but only in Kerala, not Punjab
The Green Movement was a farming subsidy scheme
discovery.answer: They merged two different things — the Green Movement is the post-1972 environmental conscience; the Green Revolution was the 1960s farm technology
discovery.hook: Two 'greens,' opposite directions — one fed the world quickly, the other asked what that feeding cost the planet.

c11_eng_h_ch05.mission: Read Palkhivala's essay as a legal brief — thesis, evidence, authorities, verdict — and spot where he borrows Thatcher's 'life tenancy' and Brown's 'borrowed from our children.'
c11_eng_h_ch05.finale: A constitutional lawyer argued the planet's case like a court brief — and the verdict he wants is a duty, not a donation.
c11_eng_h_ch05.subtitle: Tell the Green Movement from the Green Revolution — then read an essay built like a closing argument.
c11_eng_h_ch05.role: a jury member hearing the planet's case
c11_eng_h_ch05.intro: The patient says 'I feel fine'; the blood tests show organ failure. Palkhivala is the doctor-lawyer presenting the chart.
c11_eng_h_ch05.goal: Situate the Green Movement historically and analyse the essay's argumentative structure.

discovery.question: Why is the play called 'The Browning Version'? It can't only be about a Greek translation.
options: It works three ways — Browning's Agamemnon is Crocker-Harris's project, and he himself is a 'browned' version of a teacher, dried hard by disappointment
It refers only to the book Taplow gifts him
Browning wrote the play under a pseudonym
It is the school's motto, borrowed from Browning
discovery.answer: It works three ways — Browning's Agamemnon is Crocker-Harris's project, and he himself is a 'browned' version of a teacher, dried hard by disappointment
discovery.hook: The gift lands because the title was always about him — a man translated into a harder version of himself, finally read kindly.

c11_eng_h_ch06.mission: Track how a single room, a few visitors and some dialogue build a lifetime of failure — then place the true climax: the gift, or the final speech.
c11_eng_h_ch06.finale: In a one-act play, structure is character — every entrance forces someone to reveal what they'd rather hide.
c11_eng_h_ch06.subtitle: Unpack a title that names both a translation and a teacher's hardened soul.
c11_eng_h_ch06.role: a director staging a one-act play in one room
c11_eng_h_ch06.intro: A boy waits for a master who will never arrive — and forty compressed minutes expose twenty years of disappointment.
c11_eng_h_ch06.goal: Interpret the play's layered title and analyse how dramatic structure works through speech acts.

discovery.question: Professor Gaitonde wakes in a Bombay where the Marathas won Panipat. Did he travel back to 1761?
options: No — he shifted to a parallel present where that past unfolded differently; he never left his own century
Yes — the truck collision sent his body to 1761
Yes — but only his mind travelled, in a dream
No — he hallucinated while comatose, and the story says so
discovery.answer: No — he shifted to a parallel present where that past unfolded differently; he never left his own century
discovery.hook: Not time travel but a sidestep — many-worlds says another 'now' exists where Panipat went the other way.

c11_eng_h_ch07.mission: Separate the frame story from the inner alternate history, map the Bombay episode onto five dramatic stages, and judge whether Rajendra's physics is real resolution or decoration.
c11_eng_h_ch07.finale: Narlikar the astrophysicist smuggled real theory into fiction — the torn Bakhar page is the clue that refuses to stay a dream.
c11_eng_h_ch07.subtitle: Distinguish a parallel present from time travel in a scientist's alternate history.
c11_eng_h_ch07.role: a physicist auditing a historian's two missing days
c11_eng_h_ch07.intro: A truck, a blackout, and a Bombay where the East India Company still stands — explain it without calling it a dream.
c11_eng_h_ch07.goal: Explain the story's frame structure and the scientific ideas powering its alternate history.

discovery.question: Middleton drives a modern highway toward Mount Kailash — so why is the account called 'Silk Road'?
options: The route retraces ancient paths, and the 'silk' now traded is stories, beliefs and human connection
He was smuggling silk along NH 219
The title is ironic — the region never saw the real Silk Road
Pilgrims still carry bolts of silk to Kailash
discovery.answer: The route retraces ancient paths, and the 'silk' now traded is stories, beliefs and human connection
discovery.hook: The old road moved fabric; Middleton's road moves meaning — same track, different cargo.

c11_eng_h_ch08.mission: Order the journey — Ravu to Hor to Darchen to the pass — and separate the action from the reflective pauses inside the linear timeline.
c11_eng_h_ch08.finale: A travelogue can be a straight line on the map and still move in circles inside the traveller's head.
c11_eng_h_ch08.subtitle: Follow a geographer's pilgrimage where description is not the absence of plot.
c11_eng_h_ch08.role: a traveller-log analyst riding to Kailash
c11_eng_h_ch08.intro: Altitude headaches, a grim town called Hor, a stranger named Norbu — the plot is the road, but the meaning is in the pauses.
c11_eng_h_ch08.goal: Trace the travelogue's linear-yet-layered structure and read its title as metaphor.

discovery.question: Three stanzas, three different times: a girl on a beach, a mother laughing at the photo, a poet in silence. Which stanza is the climax?
options: The second — the mother's laughter at the photo, where joy and the ache of lost time collide
The first — the photograph being taken is the peak event
The third — the mother's death is the climax
None — a photograph has no plot to climax
discovery.answer: The second — the mother's laughter at the photo, where joy and the ache of lost time collide
discovery.hook: The poem isn't describing an object — it's a story memory tells in jumps: the day captured, the woman who laughed at it, the silence she left.

c11_eng_h_ch09.mission: Mark the time period each stanza inhabits, place the arc's stages, and test whether the three-stanza shape itself enacts transience.
c11_eng_h_ch09.finale: Each stanza is a world that has already vanished — the form doesn't just state the theme, it performs it.
c11_eng_h_ch09.subtitle: Watch a poem hold three times in one cardboard frame.
c11_eng_h_ch09.role: a reader holding a photograph that outlived its subject
c11_eng_h_ch09.intro: A faded beach holiday: the child in it grew up, laughed at it, and is gone — and the poet is left with the looking.
c11_eng_h_ch09.goal: Read the poem as a narrative across time frames and connect its structure to transience.

discovery.question: Is 'The Voice of the Rain' basically a science lesson about the water cycle dressed in personification?
options: No — the cycle is the vehicle; the real subject is poetry's own eternal return, rising from earth and giving back transformed
Yes — Whitman wrote it to teach evaporation and condensation
No — the rain is merely describing weather, nothing more
Yes — the personification is decoration on meteorology
discovery.answer: No — the cycle is the vehicle; the real subject is poetry's own eternal return, rising from earth and giving back transformed
discovery.hook: 'I am the Poem of Earth' — the rain narrates the water cycle so the poet can describe himself: experience rising, changing, returning.

c11_eng_h_ch10.mission: Map each stanza to its water-cycle stage and speaker, then argue why the poem needs a dialogue, not a monologue.
c11_eng_h_ch10.finale: The question 'who art thou?' makes the rain a mystery to be unveiled — cut it, and the eternal voice has no one to answer.
c11_eng_h_ch10.subtitle: Hear a water cycle talk — and notice it is describing poetry itself.
c11_eng_h_ch10.role: an interviewer granted one question to a shower
c11_eng_h_ch10.intro: The poet asks the rain who it is; the rain answers in a perfect circle — rise, transform, descend, begin again.
c11_eng_h_ch10.goal: Interpret the rain's speech as a metaphor for poetic creation and analyse the dialogue structure.

discovery.question: For three stanzas the speaker asks 'when did my childhood go?' — then the question changes. To what, and why does it matter?
options: To 'where' — childhood isn't a lost moment in time but a relocated place, 'hidden in an infant's face'
To 'why' — he finally demands the cause of growing up
To 'how' — he wants the mechanism of maturity
It doesn't — the same question repeats to the end
discovery.answer: To 'where' — childhood isn't a lost moment in time but a relocated place, 'hidden in an infant's face'
discovery.hook: Each stanza offers a different 'when' — adult hypocrisy, independent thought, a mind of one's own — then the pivot rejects 'when' altogether.

c11_eng_h_ch11.mission: Line up the poem's three candidate answers for when childhood ends, then evaluate whether the infant's face resolves the quest or deepens its irony.
c11_eng_h_ch11.finale: Childhood doesn't die — it emigrates. The speaker can see it in an infant's face but never move back in.
c11_eng_h_ch11.subtitle: Track a lyric that argues, not narrates — and watch its question mutate at the end.
c11_eng_h_ch11.role: a detective of one's own lost innocence
c11_eng_h_ch11.intro: No plot, no characters — just a man interrogating himself about the exact moment he stopped being a child.
c11_eng_h_ch11.goal: Read the poem as a cumulative philosophical argument and analyse the when-to-where pivot.

discovery.question: A classmate calls the ending 'weak' — father and son never speak or reconcile on the page. Is a silent ending a failed one?
options: No — the open denouement resolves tension without plot closure, mirroring how generational distance often stays unspoken
Yes — a story owes its readers explicit reconciliation
Yes — silence means nothing happened
No — but only because a sequel was planned
discovery.answer: No — the open denouement resolves tension without plot closure, mirroring how generational distance often stays unspoken
discovery.hook: Resolution of plot and resolution of tension aren't the same — a shared silence can close a poem better than dialogue.

c11_eng_h_ch12.mission: Treat each stanza as a film scene, find where enjambment rushes the climax, and test whether biography explains the tight quatrains holding emotional chaos.
c11_eng_h_ch12.finale: Movement poets put chaos in controlled stanzas — the form is the father trying to hold himself together.
c11_eng_h_ch12.subtitle: Read a generational silence as structure, not as a missing scene.
c11_eng_h_ch12.role: a critic weighing a poem that ends without a handshake
c11_eng_h_ch12.intro: Same house, same blood, no words — a father watches his son become someone he can't reach.
c11_eng_h_ch12.goal: Analyse narrative structure in lyric poetry and defend the open denouement.

discovery.question: Mourad has the neighbour's missing horse but insists it isn't stealing — 'it wouldn't become stealing until we offered to sell.' By his own tribe's code, is he right?
options: No — the Garoghlanian reputation for honesty is absolute, and his rule is a child's rationalisation
Yes — borrowing for joy isn't theft in any moral system
Yes — the code only forbids selling stolen goods
No — but only because John Byro actually recognised the horse
discovery.answer: No — the Garoghlanian reputation for honesty is absolute, and his rule is a child's rationalisation
discovery.hook: 'Proud first, honest next' — the boys' loophole collapses the moment Mourad himself snaps, 'Are you inviting a member of the Garoghlanian family to steal?'

c11_eng_s_ch01.mission: Separate the adult narrator's nostalgia from nine-year-old Aram's excuses, order the events chronologically, and place the real moment of moral reckoning.
c11_eng_s_ch01.finale: The horse goes back not because anyone was caught, but because the tribe's name couldn't survive being caught.
c11_eng_s_ch01.subtitle: Test a boy's loophole logic against a tribe's absolute honesty.
c11_eng_s_ch01.role: a reader untangling a childhood memory from its excuses
c11_eng_s_ch01.intro: A stolen horse ridden at dawn by a boy who swears it isn't theft — the adult telling the story knows better, and so does the tribe.
c11_eng_s_ch01.goal: Analyse the retrospective frame and evaluate the boys' moral reasoning against the Garoghlanian code.

discovery.question: Mrs. Dorling 'safekeeps' a Jewish family's belongings and later won't let the daughter in. Simple greed — or something larger?
options: Larger — she embodies the legalised seizure of Jewish property under occupation, not just one woman's dishonesty
Simple greed — a neighbour exploiting a friendship
Neither — she was protecting the items from damage
Larger — she was a paid government custodian by law
discovery.answer: Larger — she embodies the legalised seizure of Jewish property under occupation, not just one woman's dishonesty
discovery.hook: Reading her as merely greedy shrinks systemic dispossession into personal villainy — the law itself made the theft respectable.

c11_eng_s_ch02.mission: Split the story into its pre-war and post-war timeframes, place the flashbacks as structural pillars, and defend the choice to 'forget the address.'
c11_eng_s_ch02.finale: The objects were real; the life they belonged to was not reclaimable — forgetting the address is the only honest resolution left.
c11_eng_s_ch02.subtitle: Read a doorstep rejection as the machinery of dispossession, not a quarrel over furniture.
c11_eng_s_ch02.role: a survivor returning to claim a stolen past
c11_eng_s_ch02.intro: Number 46 still stands, the tablecloth is hers, the burn mark familiar — yet the room feels like a stranger's house.
c11_eng_s_ch02.goal: Situate the story in occupied Holland and analyse how its two-visit structure delivers disillusionment.

discovery.question: Mrs. Pearson gets her family to play rummy and share the chores — is the mother's exploitation actually solved?
options: No — it's a comedic compromise; the family clusters round her again, the structure intact with slightly better manners
Yes — shared chores permanently fix the power imbalance
Yes — the spell changed the family for good
No — because the swap was never real
discovery.answer: No — it's a comedic compromise; the family clusters round her again, the structure intact with slightly better manners
discovery.hook: The body-swap isn't magic solving a problem — it's the visible shape of a decision: 'this is where your foot goes down.'

c11_eng_s_ch03.mission: Rank the three confrontations — Doris, Cyril, George — on the rising curve, and judge whether the second swap earns the ending.
c11_eng_s_ch03.finale: The magic never fixed anything; it only let everyone watch what Mrs. Pearson's foot finally going down looks like.
c11_eng_s_ch03.subtitle: Read a body-swap as enacted resolve, and an ending as negotiated truce.
c11_eng_s_ch03.role: a dramatist watching a suburban mother revolt politely
c11_eng_s_ch03.intro: A meek mother starts smoking, insults her daughter's boyfriend and exposes 'Pompy-ompy Pearson' — something has clearly swapped.
c11_eng_s_ch03.goal: Analyse the play's escalating confrontations and evaluate its comedic resolution.

discovery.question: The baby is delivered at last — and lies lifeless. Many readers call the birth the climax. Where does the true turning point fall?
options: The resuscitation — the child's first cry is the irreversible pivot of both the medical and Andrew's identity arcs
The delivery — biggest event equals climax
The injection that saves the mother
Walking home at dawn — the quiet ending resolves everything
discovery.answer: The resuscitation — the child's first cry is the irreversible pivot of both the medical and Andrew's identity arcs
discovery.hook: The delivery creates a crisis instead of ending one — climax is the turn, not the title event.

c11_eng_s_ch04.mission: Map injection, resuscitation, first cry and the dawn walk onto the arc, and defend an ending that skips the mother's recovery.
c11_eng_s_ch04.finale: Andrew walks home having 'done something real at last' — the arc belonged to the doctor, not the delivery.
c11_eng_s_ch04.subtitle: Find why the story's climax is a gasp, not a birth.
c11_eng_s_ch04.role: a young doctor fighting a stillborn case at midnight
c11_eng_s_ch04.intro: A miner's cottage, no equipment, a stillborn child and a fading mother — and a doctor who arrived doubting his own profession.
c11_eng_s_ch04.goal: Place the true climax and explain why the resolution follows Andrew's arc, not the Morgans'.

discovery.question: A 'just and placid' king orders an arch, blames everyone for its failure, and ends up hanged by his own decree. What mechanism delivers this absurdity?
options: Procedure obeyed to the letter — 'someone must be hanged' and only his neck fits the arch's measure
A palace coup disguised as justice
The crowd's random fury
A prophecy that demanded a royal death
discovery.answer: Procedure obeyed to the letter — 'someone must be hanged' and only his neck fits the arch's measure
discovery.hook: The blame chain isn't random — each defence narrows the target until the king's own rule turns the noose on him.

c11_eng_s_ch05.mission: Trace the blame chain from builders to king, check whether the poem opens in medias res, and weigh whether the melon on the throne is earned or arbitrary.
c11_eng_s_ch05.finale: Sing-song couplets carry a hanging and a crowned melon — the nursery-rhyme form is the joke that makes the satire bite.
c11_eng_s_ch05.subtitle: Follow a law so rigid it executes its own king — and a people who accept a melon.
c11_eng_s_ch05.role: a satirist auditing a kingdom run by procedure
c11_eng_s_ch05.intro: An arch too low, a decree too absolute, a noose measured to fit — watch justice turn in a perfect circle.
c11_eng_s_ch05.goal: Analyse the poem's circular causal structure and the satirical work of its verse form.

discovery.question: A cabdriver's son has died and he can't get a single passenger to listen. Where does Chekhov place the climax — the shouting drunks, or somewhere quieter?
options: The quiet turn inward — after the last fare leaves, his grief 'rends his heart with greater force' and he sees the totality of his isolation
The brawl with the three young men — loudest scene equals climax
The officer's first call for a cab
The stable scene, because that's where the story ends
discovery.answer: The quiet turn inward — after the last fare leaves, his grief 'rends his heart with greater force' and he sees the totality of his isolation
discovery.hook: The rowdy passengers are noise on the way up — in a story of character, the climax is a realisation, not a collision.

c11_eng_w_ch01.mission: Mark each fare as a failed attempt to speak, find the internal climax, and decide whether the circular ending on the horse is stasis or release.
c11_eng_w_ch01.finale: He finally tells the whole story — to a horse. The circle closes, but the grief has moved from suppressed to spoken.
c11_eng_w_ch01.subtitle: Find the climax inside a grieving man, not in the loudest scene.
c11_eng_w_ch01.role: a listener shadowing an invisible cabdriver
c11_eng_w_ch01.intro: Twilight snow, a phantom cabby, a son newly buried — everyone rides, nobody hears.
c11_eng_w_ch01.goal: Distinguish a story of character from a story of incident and locate its internal climax.

discovery.question: Two confrontations over one moustache tip: the first costs a nose-ring, the second costs everything Khan Azam Khan owns. Which is the climax?
options: The second — Khan stakes all his worldly possessions and loses permanently; loudness isn't the measure
The first — it has the fiercer dialogue and open threats
Neither — the climax is the moustache hierarchy being explained
The second — but only because the elders witness the deed
discovery.answer: The second — Khan stakes all his worldly possessions and loses permanently; loudness isn't the measure
discovery.hook: Ramanand yields in round one and loses nothing real; the climax is where the stakes become irreversible.

c11_eng_w_ch02.mission: Map both confrontations onto the arc, then weigh the last line — 'My father was a Sultan' — as resolution or the cycle restarting.
c11_eng_w_ch02.finale: The moustache tips stay down, the heirlooms change hands, and the loser walks off inventing royal blood — the performance never ends.
c11_eng_w_ch02.subtitle: Watch facial hair become a caste certificate men will bankrupt themselves over.
c11_eng_w_ch02.role: a satirist decoding a village's moustache politics
c11_eng_w_ch02.intro: A moneylender dares to curl his moustache like a tiger's — and an impoverished Khan calls it theft of birthright.
c11_eng_w_ch02.goal: Analyse the doubled confrontation structure and the story's ironic non-resolution.

discovery.question: Paul wins eighty thousand pounds on the Derby — and dies immediately after. Why would Lawrence deny the story its happy ending?
options: To make the acquisition of money literally fatal — the whisper's promise that luck brings more money becomes a deadly irony
Because the author disliked tidy resolutions
To punish the uncle for betting on a child
Because Paul's gift was the real ending all along
discovery.answer: To make the acquisition of money literally fatal — the whisper's promise that luck brings more money becomes a deadly irony
discovery.hook: The climax isn't the race result — it's the frenzied ride the night before, where Paul forces the 'knowing' out of a wooden horse.

c11_eng_w_ch03.mission: Track the whispering house as the story's engine, place the true climax on the last ride, and test whether the opening counts as in medias res.
c11_eng_w_ch03.finale: The house kept whispering 'there must be more money' — the story ends by showing exactly what more money costs.
c11_eng_w_ch03.subtitle: Follow a whisper through a house to a fatal Derby win.
c11_eng_w_ch03.role: a reader inside a house that keeps asking for money
c11_eng_w_ch03.intro: A boy rides a rocking-horse furiously and names winners; the family calls it luck. Count what the luck is fed.
c11_eng_w_ch03.goal: Identify the structural climax and evaluate how the ending serves the critique of materialism.

discovery.question: Most of this Holmes story follows a hunt for a third man named Garrideb to claim millions. What is the plot actually about?
options: Luring a collector out of his room so a killer can reach the counterfeiting press buried beneath it
A genuine inheritance shared by three men with a rare surname
A legal dispute over an American estate
A missing-persons case solved by advertisement
discovery.answer: Luring a collector out of his room so a killer can reach the counterfeiting press buried beneath it
discovery.hook: The story is a double helix — Watson chases the whimsical fake plot while Holmes reads the real one in an American spelling and a frayed coat.

c11_eng_w_ch04.mission: Split the false inheritance trail from the true criminal plot, then place the inciting incident, the Birmingham trick and the cellar climax.
c11_eng_w_ch04.finale: The absurdity was the bait — a 'whimsical' will lowered a collector's guard better than any robbery could.
c11_eng_w_ch04.subtitle: See through the inheritance story to the press under the floorboards.
c11_eng_w_ch04.role: Watson, narrating a case he misunderstood until the end
c11_eng_w_ch04.intro: An American lawyer, a name worth millions, a harmless recluse — Holmes hears the counterfeiters' machinery already turning.
c11_eng_w_ch04.goal: Separate the decoy plot from the real one and map the story's structural beats.

discovery.question: Are the pigeons in 'Pigeons at Daybreak' just set dressing while the real story is a father and son?
options: No — the pigeons anchor all three structural nodes: the routine, the panic of the confrontation, and the altered ritual at the end
Yes — the title is decorative and the plot is the son's visit
No — the pigeons are the literal antagonists of the story
Yes — the birds only establish that the man is old
discovery.answer: No — the pigeons anchor all three structural nodes: the routine, the panic of the confrontation, and the altered ritual at the end
discovery.hook: A motif that returns at exposition, climax and resolution isn't decoration — it's the story's pulse.

c11_eng_w_ch05.mission: Trace the pigeon motif through the arc's nodes and show how the resumed morning ritual has quietly changed by the end.
c11_eng_w_ch05.finale: He feeds the pigeons again at daybreak — same gesture, different man; the motif records what the plot can't say.
c11_eng_w_ch05.subtitle: Read the pigeons as the story's structural heartbeat, not its wallpaper.
c11_eng_w_ch05.role: a reader tracking a motif through one morning routine
c11_eng_w_ch05.intro: An old man, a rooftop of pigeons, a son's visit that cracks the routine — watch the birds mirror what he can't say.
c11_eng_w_ch05.goal: Distinguish plot summary from structural analysis and read a recurring motif.

discovery.question: The story is set in 1969 — is the moon landing just a date stamp for flavour?
options: No — it's a structural engine: Mrs. Croft's nightly 'Splendid!' ritual over the flag becomes the bridge between a 103-year-old widow and a new immigrant
Yes — it only fixes the year for exam purposes
No — but only because Lahiri herself watched it
Yes — it's a metaphor with no function in the plot
discovery.answer: No — it's a structural engine: Mrs. Croft's nightly 'Splendid!' ritual over the flag becomes the bridge between a 103-year-old widow and a new immigrant
discovery.hook: The narrator isn't Lahiri, and the moon isn't trivia — both are deliberate architecture: a flag on the moon lets two strangers share a country.

c11_eng_w_ch06.mission: Order India, London and Boston as one continuous preparation — then place the climax where the narrator's two worlds finally meet over 'Splendid!'
c11_eng_w_ch06.finale: Three continents aren't three stories — each one trains him for the next, and the last frame drives his son past the street where America began for him.
c11_eng_w_ch06.subtitle: See a moon landing become the handshake between an old Yankee and a new immigrant.
c11_eng_w_ch06.role: an immigrant measuring three continents of displacement
c11_eng_w_ch06.intro: Calcutta to a London boarding house to a Boston room with a centenarian landlady — the rent was inconceivable; so was staying.
c11_eng_w_ch06.goal: Read the three-continent structure as cumulative growth and evaluate the circular frame.

discovery.question: Satyajit's bank has already collapsed when the story opens on a slow train — so where can the climax possibly be?
options: At the wedding — when he signs away his house and pond for a stranger's dowry, the last of the glory spent
In the bank collapse itself, told in flashback
On the train, when he asks 'What now?'
At the fig tree, where he finally rests
discovery.answer: At the wedding — when he signs away his house and pond for a stranger's dowry, the last of the glory spent
discovery.hook: Chronological climax and narrative climax are different events — the story peaks where the pretending becomes impossible to afford.

c11_eng_w_ch07.mission: Separate the train frame from the flashbacks, order the narrative versus chronological events, and place the deed-signing as the true climax.
c11_eng_w_ch07.finale: The village worships a success that was born from a forger's crime and dies at a dowry table — the flashbacks make both ironies visible at once.
c11_eng_w_ch07.subtitle: Watch a fallen banker's borrowed glory spend itself to the last rupee.
c11_eng_w_ch07.role: a reader watching a reputation burn like a twilight sky
c11_eng_w_ch07.intro: A narrow-gauge train making unauthorised stops, a collapsed bank, and a village still expecting benediction in cash.
c11_eng_w_ch07.goal: Distinguish frame from flashback and locate the narrative climax of a non-linear story.

discovery.question: Ruined by a luncheon he couldn't refuse, the narrator ends with a joke: 'I'll eat nothing for dinner tonight.' Is that growth?
options: No — it's performative deflection; twenty years later the telling itself is his cold revenge
Yes — humour shows he finally matured past the humiliation
Yes — he learned to say no to women
No — because he never paid the bill
discovery.answer: No — it's performative deflection; twenty years later the telling itself is his cold revenge
discovery.hook: He still couldn't say no in the restaurant — the only 'revenge' available was narrating her into twenty-one stone, two decades on.

c11_eng_w_ch08.mission: Separate the twenty-years-later frame from the flashback, rank the escalating orders from salmon to peaches, and place the true climax at the bill.
c11_eng_w_ch08.finale: Each dish she 'never minds' is a step deeper into his panic — the menu is the rising action.
c11_eng_w_ch08.subtitle: Watch a month's budget get eaten course by course — and revenge arrive twenty years late.
c11_eng_w_ch08.role: a diarist dissecting a ruinous lunch in 1920s Paris
c11_eng_w_ch08.intro: Eighty francs was survival money for a month — and the lady 'never minds' caviare.
c11_eng_w_ch08.goal: Analyse the retrospective frame and the escalating structure of Maugham's anecdote.

discovery.question: Sujata Bhatt writes India's national bird while living in Germany. A critic calls it 'a foreigner's exotic view — not an authentic Indian poem.' Fair?
options: No — diaspora produces differently positioned truth; the poem's honesty about distance is its authenticity
Yes — only residents can write national symbols authentically
Yes — her Gujarati is too rusty to claim the subject
No — because peacocks also exist in European zoos
discovery.answer: No — diaspora produces differently positioned truth; the poem's honesty about distance is its authenticity
discovery.hook: The poem doesn't pretend the peacock is in the room — it's a 'blue shadow' falling on someone reading, glimpsed across a gap the poem refuses to hide.

c11_eng_w_ch09.mission: Order the sensory signals that announce the bird — shadow, wind, silenced bees, stretching cat — then judge whether free verse mimics its darting.
c11_eng_w_ch09.finale: The poem's ragged lines move the way the bird does — appearing, vanishing, leaving only the very end of a tail.
c11_eng_w_ch09.subtitle: Read a diaspora poem where distance is the subject, not the defect.
c11_eng_w_ch09.role: a reader catching a blue shadow at the edge of a page
c11_eng_w_ch09.intro: A veranda, a book, a hush — the peacock is announced by everything except its own body.
c11_eng_w_ch09.goal: Evaluate diasporic perspective and read the poem's sensory progression as structure.

discovery.question: 'If this be error and upon me proved, / I never writ, nor no man ever loved.' Logical proof of his definition — or a trap?
options: A rhetorical trap — to refute him you'd have to prove he never wrote or that nobody ever loved, an impossible burden
A watertight logical proof of true love's constancy
A confession that his definition is probably wrong
A legal loophole admitting exceptions
discovery.answer: A rhetorical trap — to refute him you'd have to prove he never wrote or that nobody ever loved, an impossible burden
discovery.hook: The sonnet argues like a lawyer — define by negation, turn at 'O no, it is an ever-fixed mark,' then stake everything on a verdict no one can overturn.

c11_eng_w_ch10.mission: Mark the ABAB CDCD EFEF GG skeleton, find the volta at line 9, and try building your own quatrain that argues by negation.
c11_eng_w_ch10.finale: Three quatrains to build the case, one couplet to slam the door — the sonnet's shape is the argument.
c11_eng_w_ch10.subtitle: Read a love poem that behaves like a courtroom brief.
c11_eng_w_ch10.intro: Love that 'bends with the remover to remove' gets struck from the definition — then the poet dares you to disprove him.
c11_eng_w_ch10.goal: Identify the Shakespearean sonnet's argumentative structure, volta and closing wager.

discovery.question: 'Coming' describes a thrush singing in a garden — so Larkin is a nature poet like Wordsworth, right?
options: No — Movement poets rejected Romantic nature-worship; the thrush merely 'astonishes the brickwork' of an ordinary suburb
Yes — any poem about a bird is Romantic
Yes — the garden makes it a nature poem by definition
No — Larkin only ever wrote about libraries
discovery.answer: No — Movement poets rejected Romantic nature-worship; the thrush merely 'astonishes the brickwork' of an ordinary suburb
discovery.hook: Even the song is 'fresh-peeled' — a kitchen verb, raw and domestic, not 'melodious'; Larkin refuses the poetic word on purpose.

c11_eng_w_ch11.mission: Track the poem from houses at dusk to the thrush to a childhood memory, and explain the final simile of a child stumbling on 'adult reconciling.'
c11_eng_w_ch11.finale: The bird announces spring; the speaker feels like a child who can't name the happiness — incomprehension is the point.
c11_eng_w_ch11.subtitle: Hear a thrush interrupt a suburb — and a poet who refuses to worship it.
c11_eng_w_ch11.role: a listener catching spring arrive over brickwork
c11_eng_w_ch11.intro: A bare garden, an evening, one bird — and a grown man suddenly feeling like a child who walked in on something unexplained.
c11_eng_w_ch11.goal: Situate Larkin in The Movement and read the poem's shift from observation to inner recognition.

discovery.question: Asked 'HOW DARK?' on a phone call about a flat, the speaker answers with jokes — 'plain or milk chocolate?' Does the wit weaken the protest?
options: It amplifies it — humour refuses victimhood and exposes racism's 'clinical, crushing' absurdity
It weakens it — jokes trivialise discrimination
Neither — the humour is separate from the politics
It weakens it — satire can't confront real prejudice
discovery.answer: It amplifies it — humour refuses victimhood and exposes racism's 'clinical, crushing' absurdity
discovery.hook: The telephone strips away everything but voice — so the only place racism can operate is a question about shade, and the poem dismantles it there.

c11_eng_w_ch12.mission: Find the pivot where a housing call becomes a racial negotiation, read the silences and capitals as structure, and judge the open ending.
c11_eng_w_ch12.finale: 'Wouldn't you rather see for yourself?' — he ends the call by refusing the category, leaving the door open and the verdict with her.
c11_eng_w_ch12.subtitle: Hear a rental call become a colour inspection — answered with devastating politeness.
c11_eng_w_ch12.role: a caller pricing a flat in 1960s London
c11_eng_w_ch12.intro: Price, location — agreed. Then one confession turns a transaction into an interrogation about melanin.
c11_eng_w_ch12.goal: Analyse the poem's dramatic structure and evaluate satire as a response to racism.

discovery.question: Wordsworth cries 'Great God! I'd rather be / A Pagan suckled in a creed outworn.' Is he renouncing his faith?
options: No — it's hyperbole against a society that commodifies nature; 'Pagan' means perceiving divinity in sea and wind, not atheism
Yes — he is formally converting to paganism
Yes — the sestet rejects all religion equally
No — he is only being ironic about mythology
discovery.answer: No — it's hyperbole against a society that commodifies nature; 'Pagan' means perceiving divinity in sea and wind, not atheism
discovery.hook: He addresses the Christian God while damning the Christian-age marketplace — the creed he'd swap is 'getting and spending,' not worship itself.

c11_eng_w_ch13.mission: Split the sonnet at the volta — octave as diagnosis, sestet as desperate wish — and test whether the turn could land anywhere but line 9.
c11_eng_w_ch13.finale: Eight lines to convict 'getting and spending,' six to imagine a creed that still heard the sea — the hinge is the poem's whole argument.
c11_eng_w_ch13.subtitle: Read a sonnet's turn as the hinge between diagnosis and desperation.
c11_eng_w_ch13.role: a Romantic watching a world too busy to see the sea
c11_eng_w_ch13.intro: Rush hour on a metro platform, 1802 edition — everyone 'getting and spending,' nobody feeling the wind.
c11_eng_w_ch13.goal: Identify the Petrarchan octave-sestet structure and interpret the pagan wish correctly.
