c11_hin_v_ch01.subtitle: Watch theatre's grammar shift from the spoken word to the seen image.
c11_hin_v_ch01.role: a theatre-goer learning to watch with new eyes
c11_hin_v_ch01.intro: Before the curtain: a voice from a machine, no face attached — Agyeya builds his whole argument about modern theatre from that disembodied sound.
c11_hin_v_ch01.goal: Distinguish literary and visual drama and analyse the essay's experiential-to-theoretical arc.

discovery.question: Alwar's johads brought dead wells back to life — so is water revival basically an engineering project?
options: No — johads are a social contract: caste, gender and gram-sabha power decide who builds, who shares, who is heard
Yes — dig the right pond and the water follows
Yes — runoff math is the whole problem
No — because johads are religious structures
discovery.answer: No — johads are a social contract: caste, gender and gram-sabha power decide who builds, who shares, who is heard
discovery.hook: The pond is the easy part — historically the dominant castes controlled the water; revival worked only when women's jal sabhas rewrote the sharing rules.

c11_hin_v_ch02.mission: Compute a catchment-to-command ratio for a village, then follow the chapter's escalation from grain-share to cash wage to piece-rate labour.
c11_hin_v_ch02.finale: The text ends not with a policy memo but trickling streams merging into sweet water — small flows self-organising into abundance is the whole argument.
c11_hin_v_ch02.subtitle: See a pond as a village's constitution, not its engineering.
c11_hin_v_ch02.role: a village deciding who owns the rain
c11_hin_v_ch02.intro: Tankers queue at the municipal tap while the old johad sits dry — the difference between them was never concrete, it was cooperation.
c11_hin_v_ch02.goal: Read the johad system as social institution and analyse the chapter's inductive structure.

discovery.question: 'Sobti wrote this to show how hard life was for poor women in the 1950s' — what does that reading miss?
options: That autobiographical fiction is crafted, not documented — blurred author-narrator lines, fragmented memory, and tactical silence are the strategy
Nothing — it's plain social reporting
That she invented the suffering entirely
That domestic work was actually easy then
discovery.answer: That autobiographical fiction is crafted, not documented — blurred author-narrator lines, fragmented memory, and tactical silence are the strategy
discovery.hook: The protagonist performs the 'good servant' when it suits her and refuses questions when it doesn't — resistance here is tactical, not absolute.

c11_hin_v_ch03.mission: Find the inciting incident — the lawyer's wife handing over a notebook — and defend the climax where a servant reads her own story aloud.
c11_hin_v_ch03.finale: The notebook and pen turn a worker into an author — the climax isn't publication, it's being heard by the person who gave them.
c11_hin_v_ch03.subtitle: Watch a domestic worker cross the line from serving stories to writing one.
c11_hin_v_ch03.role: a reader inside a Partition-displaced woman's first-person voice
c11_hin_v_ch03.intro: A widowed domestic worker in a lawyer's Delhi household gets a notebook — and the household's power arrangement quietly inverts.
c11_hin_v_ch03.goal: Analyse autobiographical fiction's blurred boundaries and the story's arc toward self-expression.

discovery.question: 'The more local an art is in its expression, the more universal it becomes' — can that paradox actually hold?
options: Yes — Warli's rice-paste spirals use only circle, triangle and square: the most local cosmology drawn in the most universal shapes
No — local art stays local by definition
Yes — but only after foreigners validate it
No — universality requires abandoning the local
discovery.answer: Yes — Warli's rice-paste spirals use only circle, triangle and square: the most local cosmology drawn in the most universal shapes
discovery.hook: Folk and classical aren't two boxes — Kathak grew out of kathavachaks and temple dances sank back into villages; the continuum never stops trading.

c11_hin_v_ch04.mission: Trace how the essay runs every art form through the same folk→classical→living-continuity arc, and judge what that repeated pattern proves.
c11_hin_v_ch04.finale: Bhimbetka's cave lines, a Rajasthani wall at Diwali, a Tanjore court repertoire — one argument repeated until it becomes evidence.
c11_hin_v_ch04.subtitle: Test the claim that the most local art travels the farthest.
c11_hin_v_ch04.role: a reader mapping Indian art's hidden continuum
c11_hin_v_ch04.intro: Mandana on a mud wall in a village, Kathak in a Jaipur auditorium — the essay asks what these share, not what divides them.
c11_hin_v_ch04.goal: Analyse the folk-classical continuum and the essay's classification-driven structure.

discovery.question: A Rajput tale has a widow choose jauhar and a steward bankrupt himself for his lord — madness, or a code you're missing?
options: A code — maru-maryada, jauhar and bhamashah are implicit rules that make 'irrational' sacrifice read as honour
Madness — no rational person chooses death
A code — but only kings followed it
Madness — folk tales aren't bound by logic
discovery.answer: A code — maru-maryada, jauhar and bhamashah are implicit rules that make 'irrational' sacrifice read as honour
discovery.hook: Vishnu Prabhakar worked the Rajasthan State Archives for decades — these aren't fairy tales but itihaas, history as the people witnessed it.

c11_hin_v_ch05.mission: Match archival motifs (jauhar, sakha, bhamashah) to the folk narratives, then weigh why the story's trauma stays unresolved at the end.
c11_hin_v_ch05.finale: The archive and the bard tell the same past in different inks — folk narrative is history that refused to be filed away.
c11_hin_v_ch05.subtitle: Read Rajasthani folk tales as a people's archive of honour codes.
c11_hin_v_ch05.role: an archivist cross-checking ballads against records
c11_hin_v_ch05.intro: Desert kingdoms, bards, and sacrifices that look irrational — until you learn the code they're written in.
c11_hin_v_ch05.goal: Decode the cultural rules inside Rajasthani folk narratives and analyse their non-linear structure.

discovery.question: Southern Mesopotamia was a desert with under 150 mm of rain — yet it produced the world's first cities. How?
options: Human-engineered irrigation plus temple institutions that mobilised surplus — not natural bounty
The desert was secretly fertile crescent land
Rivers alone made farming effortless
Kings built cities first and writing followed their glory
discovery.answer: Human-engineered irrigation plus temple institutions that mobilised surplus — not natural bounty
discovery.hook: And writing didn't start with royal boasting — the earliest tablets are temple accounts; kings like Enmerkar adopted the tablet, they didn't invent it.

c11_hist_ch01.mission: Draw the resource flows between mountain, steppe and desert zones, then trace clay tokens into syllabic cuneiform — a script, not a language.
c11_hist_ch01.finale: A desert farmed by canals and a temple keeping ration lists — the city was an accounting invention before it was an architectural one.
c11_hist_ch01.subtitle: See how a desert birthed cities — and bookkeeping birthed writing.
c11_hist_ch01.role: an archaeologist decoding Uruk's clay tablets
c11_hist_ch01.intro: Between the Tigris and Euphrates, a rainless south out-traded its resource-rich north — institutions did what geography couldn't.
c11_hist_ch01.goal: Explain how irrigation and temple economies produced cities, and how accounting produced cuneiform.

discovery.question: Did Rome expand like an ink blot, seeping outward equally in every direction?
options: No — it followed resource corridors along the Mediterranean and stopped dead at the Rhine-Danube, the Euphrates and the Sahara
Yes — empires grow uniformly in all directions
Yes — legions marched wherever they pleased
No — it only expanded east toward India
discovery.answer: No — it followed resource corridors along the Mediterranean and stopped dead at the Rhine-Danube, the Euphrates and the Sahara
discovery.hook: The sea was the empire's private highway — Spanish olive oil could undercut Italian producers 2,000 km away because 'Mare Nostrum' made bulk trade coastal and cheap.

c11_hist_ch02.mission: Compare Rome's self-governing civitates with the Maurya-appointed nagara, then test whether Augustus's Principate was a republic or a monarchy in disguise.
c11_hist_ch02.finale: Trajan watched a merchant ship leave for India with longing — the Mediterranean was a closed lake Rome owned; the Indian Ocean was a market it could only envy.
c11_hist_ch02.subtitle: Read an empire as a lake with edges — and a republic wearing a crown.
c11_hist_ch02.role: a geographer tracing where Rome stopped and why
c11_hist_ch02.intro: A city-state in Italy ended up ruling Scotland to Syria — because it owned the sea between them.
c11_hist_ch02.goal: Explain Mediterranean integration, provincial cities, and the Augustan settlement's disguise.

discovery.question: Constantine's Edict of Milan in 313 CE made Christianity Rome's official religion — settled fact?
options: No — it only legalised the faith; sole official status came 67 years later under Theodosius in 380
Yes — Milan made it the state church
Yes — Constantine himself baptised the empire
No — Christianity stayed illegal until 476
discovery.answer: No — it only legalised the faith; sole official status came 67 years later under Theodosius in 380
discovery.hook: And the third-century collapse wasn't barbarians breaking in — legions left the frontiers to fight rival emperors, and the invasions were the consequence.

c11_hist_ch03.mission: List the third century's symptoms — twenty emperors, hollowed-out coins, wall-less Rome suddenly walled — then weigh whether Diocletian's Tetrarchy truly fixed succession.
c11_hist_ch03.finale: An empire that needed emergency walls after three centuries of needing none — the crisis was the system failing, not the enemy arriving.
c11_hist_ch03.subtitle: Diagnose an empire's fifty-year fever — and a sect that outlived its persecutors.
c11_hist_ch03.role: a historian reading symptoms on an imperial chart
c11_hist_ch03.intro: Twenty emperors in fifty years, silver vanishing from the coins, walls going up around Rome — the crisis had no single cause, which is the point.
c11_hist_ch03.goal: Analyse the third-century crisis as systemic failure and trace Christianity from persecution to establishment.

discovery.question: Pre-Islamic Arabia: an isolated backwater waiting for history to begin?
options: No — Mecca sat on the incense-spice routes linking the Indian Ocean to the Mediterranean, and its sanctuary made a truce zone for trade
Yes — deserts can't support trade
Yes — only the Prophet's arrival connected it
No — because Arabia was never a desert
discovery.answer: No — Mecca sat on the incense-spice routes linking the Indian Ocean to the Mediterranean, and its sanctuary made a truce zone for trade
discovery.hook: The haram solved an economic problem religiously — a sanctuary where feuding tribes could safely do business, with Quraysh collecting the toll.

c11_hist_ch04.mission: Trace a frankincense caravan from Yemen to Gaza through Mecca's oases, then judge whether the mala' made Mecca a merchant republic.
c11_hist_ch04.finale: Tribal feuds plus caravan profits needed one invention: a sacred zone where war paused and trade could happen.
c11_hist_ch04.subtitle: Find the trade junction hiding inside a desert sanctuary.
c11_hist_ch04.role: a Quraysh merchant pricing sanctuary and water rights
c11_hist_ch04.intro: At Ajmer's Urs, pilgrimage and market blend — now strip away the Islam and you have seventh-century Mecca's whole business model.
c11_hist_ch04.goal: Explain Mecca's commercial-religious leverage and the tribal structure of pre-Islamic Arabia.

discovery.question: 'Nomad' means wandering aimlessly across empty grassland — that's what made the Mongols mobile, right?
options: No — migration followed precise multi-generational maps of named pastures and water points, timed to the greening of specific grasses
Yes — nomads moved randomly with the weather
Yes — that's why they needed no maps
No — nomads never actually moved at all
discovery.answer: No — migration followed precise multi-generational maps of named pastures and water points, timed to the greening of specific grasses
discovery.hook: And the steppe was never self-sufficient — it structurally lacked grain, metal and craft, which is why pre-Genghis graves already hold Chinese silk and Persian ceramics.

c11_hist_ch05.mission: Balance a herd of 'five snouts' for risk, then test whether the steppe economy was inherently raiding-driven or trade-connected all along.
c11_hist_ch05.finale: The largest land empire in history grew out of an ecology that couldn't feed itself — the mobility was a system, not a wandering.
c11_hist_ch05.subtitle: Meet the nomads who ran empires on a calendar of grass.
c11_hist_ch05.role: a steppe household planning the year's pastures
c11_hist_ch05.intro: Minus forty winters, no rivers, no trees — and from this the largest contiguous empire ever built. The ecology is the key.
c11_hist_ch05.goal: Explain pastoral nomadism as a mapped system and its structural dependence on settled trade.

discovery.question: Those who pray, those who fight, those who work — was Europe's three-order society a caste system like varna, fixed by birth and law?
options: No — it was an ideological model pushed by bishops: functional, porous, and blind to merchants, Jews and unfree knights who didn't fit
Yes — birth legally locked every order
Yes — both systems are identical
No — because Europe had no hierarchy at all
discovery.answer: No — it was an ideological model pushed by bishops: functional, porous, and blind to merchants, Jews and unfree knights who didn't fit
discovery.hook: The model appears in sermons to kings, not in manor records — a society 'imagined by bishops' while real towns full of merchants grew outside the schema.

c11_hist_ch06.mission: Test the three orders against real people — a merchant's son, a serf, a friar — then map how the Church became landowner, court and rival of kings.
c11_hist_ch06.finale: The real legal line wasn't pray-fight-work but free-unfree — the tidy triad was a sermon, not a census.
c11_hist_ch06.subtitle: See a tidy medieval schema collide with the messy society it described.
c11_hist_ch06.role: a canon lawyer auditing who the schema forgot
c11_hist_ch06.intro: A cathedral dominates the town — but inside the neat triad of oratores, bellatores and laboratores, the merchants building that town don't exist.
c11_hist_ch06.goal: Evaluate the three-orders model against feudal society's actual divisions and the Church's real power.

discovery.question: Constantinople fell in 1453, Greek scholars fled west — and that's what caused the Renaissance?
options: No — the Renaissance was decades underway by 1400; scholars had been arriving since the 1390s and 1453 only accelerated it
Yes — one event started the whole movement
Yes — Italy had no Greek texts before 1453
No — the Renaissance actually caused the fall
discovery.answer: No — the Renaissance was decades underway by 1400; scholars had been arriving since the 1390s and 1453 only accelerated it
discovery.hook: And the humanists weren't secular rebels — Petrarch and Erasmus were devout Christians mining classical sources to deepen faith, not escape it.

c11_hist_ch07.mission: Separate the Medici's banker-capitalism from feudal lordship, then weigh the printing press against manuscript networks in humanism's spread.
c11_hist_ch07.finale: The Renaissance ran on trade profits and merchant patronage — art was what finance bought when it looked in a mirror.
c11_hist_ch07.subtitle: Time the rebirth correctly — it started before the city fell.
c11_hist_ch07.role: a scholar tracing how Greek manuscripts reached Florence
c11_hist_ch07.intro: Statues commissioned by merchant-bankers crowd a Florentine square — why here, why then, and who actually paid for it?
c11_hist_ch07.goal: Explain the city-state conditions behind the Renaissance and humanism's relationship to Christianity.

discovery.question: A Class 11 boy skips Human Ecology and Family Sciences: 'it's cooking and stitching for girls.' Is he describing the subject correctly?
options: No — it's an interdisciplinary science of humans-in-environments, explicitly renamed to shed the gendered 'home science' tag
Yes — it's the old home science with a new label
Yes — the content never changed
No — it's only about nutrition now
discovery.answer: No — it's an interdisciplinary science of humans-in-environments, explicitly renamed to shed the gendered 'home science' tag
discovery.hook: Lady Irwin College's founders — Naidu, Amrit Kaur, Chattopadhyay — built it in 1932 for service to home AND society; the stereotype came later.

c11_hs_ch01.mission: Take an everyday dinner decision and split it into the four environments — physical, economic, social, psychological — that silently shaped it.
c11_hs_ch01.finale: Every choice you make is ecology: hunger is biology, but what's on the plate is economics, custom and mood negotiating.
c11_hs_ch01.subtitle: Discover the science hiding behind a misnamed subject.
c11_hs_ch01.role: a student decoding what HEFS actually studies
c11_hs_ch01.intro: Choosing dinner isn't just appetite — season, budget, festival and stress all vote. That negotiation is the subject.
c11_hs_ch01.goal: Define human ecology's multi-dimensional environment and dispel the domestic-skills stereotype.

discovery.question: Two students write the same self-description — 'average in studies, good at painting, short-tempered.' One feels fine, one feels a failure. Same self-concept, different what?
options: Different self-esteem — worth is measured against each one's internalised ideal self, not against the description
Different memory — they recall different events
Different intelligence — one is more honest
Different personality type — optimist versus pessimist
discovery.answer: Different self-esteem — worth is measured against each one's internalised ideal self, not against the description
discovery.hook: And 'I am a daughter, a sister, a Rajput' isn't a weaker self — Indian selves often speak in 'we,' and that's interdependence, not deficiency.

c11_hs_ch02.mission: Sort 'I am' statements into bodily, emotional, mental, social and agentic selves, then test why positive affirmations can backfire.
c11_hs_ch02.finale: Self-concept is the description; self-esteem is the gap between it and the standard you absorbed — change the standard and the same you scores differently.
c11_hs_ch02.subtitle: Split the description of you from the verdict on you.
c11_hs_ch02.role: a counsellor separating what a teen is from what they demand of themselves
c11_hs_ch02.intro: 'I am lazy' is a description; 'I am worthless' is a verdict — and they don't come from the same place.
c11_hs_ch02.goal: Distinguish self-concept from self-esteem and read the cultural 'we-self' correctly.

discovery.question: A school serves calorie-adequate mid-day meals, yet a third of the children stay undernourished after a year. The food failed — or did something else?
options: Something else — caste seating, disliked taste and who eats last at home all sit between adequate food and an adequately fed child
The food — adequate calories always nourish
The children — they chose to be undernourished
The calories — the count was surely wrong
discovery.answer: Something else — caste seating, disliked taste and who eats last at home all sit between adequate food and an adequately fed child
discovery.hook: Nutrition science isn't just biology — the social, psychological and economic dimensions aren't add-ons; they're where meals actually fail.

c11_hs_ch03.mission: Classify roti, spinach, ghee and iodised salt by the grams-versus-micrograms rule, then break the claim that one food or one calorie number can fix malnutrition.
c11_hs_ch03.finale: No single food carries everything — rice gives energy but hides no vitamin C; variety is a design rule, not a luxury.
c11_hs_ch03.subtitle: See why identical lunches produce different bodies — food is biology plus society.
c11_hs_ch03.role: a nutritionist auditing a program that should have worked
c11_hs_ch03.intro: Same tray, same calories, different outcomes — the science of nutrition starts where the lunch line ends.
c11_hs_ch03.goal: Classify nutrients by requirement scale and apply nutrition's four dimensions.

discovery.question: 'Money is the most powerful resource — it substitutes for almost everything else.' Where does this break?
options: Money can't cook the meal or motivate the child itself — no intrinsic utility, and managing it is a skill in itself
Nowhere — money substitutes for all resources
Only when the bank is closed
Only in villages without ATMs
discovery.answer: Money can't cook the meal or motivate the child itself — no intrinsic utility, and managing it is a skill in itself
discovery.hook: A dusty bicycle isn't a resource until a goal turns it into one — resources are defined by intentional use, not by possession.

c11_hs_ch04.mission: Classify a skill, a metro system and a rainwater tank across human/non-human, individual/shared and natural/community — then let the categories shift with the goal.
c11_hs_ch04.finale: Aptitude isn't skill and skill isn't motivation — four human resources, and the weakest one caps the rest.
c11_hs_ch04.subtitle: Learn when a thing becomes a resource — and why money isn't one of them by itself.
c11_hs_ch04.role: a planner auditing what a family can actually use
c11_hs_ch04.intro: ₹2,000, three days, a cousin's car and your mother's recipes — which of these count as resources? It depends on the party.
c11_hs_ch04.goal: Apply utility, accessibility and interchangeability to classify resources and evaluate money's limits.

discovery.question: '100% polyester — cool and comfortable for Indian summers because it wicks moisture.' Sound science?
options: No — polyester's moisture regain is ~0.4%; it can't absorb sweat, so skin stays clammy whatever the capillary marketing claims
Yes — wicking equals comfort
Yes — synthetics always beat naturals
No — polyester melts in heat
discovery.answer: No — polyester's moisture regain is ~0.4%; it can't absorb sweat, so skin stays clammy whatever the capillary marketing claims
discovery.hook: Fibre alone doesn't decide behaviour — a loose cotton voile shrinks more than tight cotton denim; yarn, weave and finish rewrite the fibre's script.

c11_hs_ch05.mission: Run a visual-plus-burn test to sort an unknown fabric into cellulosic, protein or synthetic, then spec a school-uniform blend for humidity.
c11_hs_ch05.finale: Fibre → yarn → fabric → finish: every level up the hierarchy can overrule the level below — that chain is the whole subject.
c11_hs_ch05.subtitle: Unpick a fabric claim layer by layer — fibre to finish.
c11_hs_ch05.role: a textile tester with a magnifier and a match
c11_hs_ch05.intro: A cotton kurta wrinkles and shrinks while a polyester saree survives three washes untouched — the fibre hierarchy explains why.
c11_hs_ch05.goal: Trace how fibre, yarn, weave and finish jointly determine fabric behaviour.

discovery.question: A YouTube livestream to 10,000 viewers has a chat box — so it's two-way communication, right?
options: No — the creator reads a sliver of comments and adapts for no one; technical interactivity isn't communicative reciprocity
Yes — any channel back makes it two-way
Yes — digital means interactive by definition
No — because only radio counts as one-way
discovery.answer: No — the creator reads a sliver of comments and adapts for no one; technical interactivity isn't communicative reciprocity
discovery.hook: Speaking isn't communicating — if the receiver's picture doesn't match the sender's, communication never happened; that's why feedback both starts and ends the loop.

c11_hs_ch06.mission: Classify a radio forecast, a helpline call and a WhatsApp homework thread by the feedback test, then defend where one-way still wins — cyclone sirens.
c11_hs_ch06.finale: One-way isn't inferior — when a cyclone's coming you want reach and fidelity, not a dialogue.
c11_hs_ch06.subtitle: Learn the difference between transmitting a message and sharing a meaning.
c11_hs_ch06.role: an extension worker choosing how to reach a village
c11_hs_ch06.intro: Explaining UPI to your grandmother by phone: she heard every word and pressed the wrong buttons — did communication happen?
c11_hs_ch06.goal: Apply the feedback criterion to distinguish one-way and two-way communication in extension work.

discovery.question: A student scores 95%, has no friends, feels anxious daily and gets breathless on stairs — is she healthy?
options: No — WHO defines health as complete physical, mental AND social well-being; she's failing on all three counts
Yes — she has no diagnosed disease
Yes — academic fitness is what matters
No — but only the breathlessness counts
discovery.answer: No — WHO defines health as complete physical, mental AND social well-being; she's failing on all three counts
discovery.hook: Vaccination programs fix one dimension — a jab can't counsel anxiety or seat a lonely child at a lunch table.

c11_hs_ch07.mission: Route a village child's diarrhoea through the three tiers of care, then diagnose what failed when a heart-attack patient bypassed the PHC for a medical college 80 km away.
c11_hs_ch07.finale: Each tier gatekeeps the one above — when every fever lands at AIIMS, the system fails the patient who needed it.
c11_hs_ch07.subtitle: Redefine health beyond 'not sick' — and learn why the smallest clinic guards the biggest hospital.
c11_hs_ch07.role: a health-systems planner assigning patients to tiers
c11_hs_ch07.intro: Fever at dawn — big hospital or small centre? The wrong answer costs the system, and sometimes the patient.
c11_hs_ch07.goal: Apply the WHO definition of health and India's three-tier referral system.

discovery.question: A 10-year-old lives on chips, cola and white bread — 2,500 kcal a day and overweight. Malnourished?
options: Yes — obesity with iron, calcium and vitamin D deficiency is still malnutrition; the burden runs both ways
No — overweight means over-nourished, full stop
No — malnutrition only means being thin
Yes — but only because of the sugar
discovery.answer: Yes — obesity with iron, calcium and vitamin D deficiency is still malnutrition; the burden runs both ways
discovery.hook: For a low-birth-weight baby, the fix isn't a formula bottle — mother's milk carries amino acids and antimicrobial factors no powder replicates.

c11_hs_ch08.mission: Compute a preschooler's protein and energy deficits against ICMR norms, then argue why protein shortfall cuts deeper than calorie shortfall at age four.
c11_hs_ch08.finale: Between one and six the brain is wiring itself on amino acids — an energy gap slows a child down; a protein gap builds less brain.
c11_hs_ch08.subtitle: Learn why 'well-fed' and 'well-nourished' are two different report cards.
c11_hs_ch08.role: a health worker weighing a village's children
c11_hs_ch08.intro: An infant at 4.5 kg on diluted cow's milk, a preschooler with night blindness on rice-and-dal — each stage has its own nutritional maths.
c11_hs_ch08.goal: Link feeding practices to developmental stages and evaluate the dual burden of malnutrition.

discovery.question: A bridal lehenga — modesty garment, protection garment, or status garment? Pick its function.
options: All four at once — coverage, warmth, zari-woven status and ornament; every garment multitasks and context picks the dominant one
Status — weddings are displays
Modesty — it's full-coverage
Adornment — it's decorative
discovery.answer: All four at once — coverage, warmth, zari-woven status and ornament; every garment multitasks and context picks the dominant one
discovery.hook: Which is why 'one national uniform for all of India' fails — the same cloth can't serve modesty norms in Srinagar, monsoon protection in Odisha and status-blindness everywhere.

c11_hs_ch09.mission: Spec a uniform for humid coastal Odisha across protection, modesty, status and adornment — then pack a Chennai 12-year-old for a Leh January exhibition.
c11_hs_ch09.finale: Age, climate, occasion — the three filters interact, and a garment that wins two can still fail the third.
c11_hs_ch09.subtitle: Dress for a wedding, a monsoon and a mountain — with one logic.
c11_hs_ch09.role: a wardrobe planner balancing four functions at once
c11_hs_ch09.intro: Sherwani, Pashmina, juttis for a Delhi December wedding — decode why each choice earned its place.
c11_hs_ch09.goal: Apply the four clothing functions and the age-climate-occasion filters to real selection problems.

discovery.question: Family A earns ₹1 lakh but buys everything in; Family B earns less but has a kitchen garden, a grandmother's childcare and a father's repair skills. Who's richer in living?
options: Family B — quality of living runs on real and psychic income, not money income alone
Family A — money is the only income that counts
Family A — services bought are always better
Equal — income is income
discovery.answer: Family B — quality of living runs on real and psychic income, not money income alone
discovery.hook: And a budget isn't the plan — it's the written output of one; fill in numbers without goals and you've made a spreadsheet, not a decision.

c11_hs_ch10.mission: Balance a ₹60,000 household budget against a ₹10,000 savings goal, then optimise the Sharma family's skills and time toward a ₹5 lakh admission.
c11_hs_ch10.finale: Material resources alone are concentration risk — human skill and community assets are the diversification a money-only family lacks.
c11_hs_ch10.subtitle: Count a family's wealth in three currencies, not one.
c11_hs_ch10.role: a family CFO auditing non-money income
c11_hs_ch10.intro: Renovate the kitchen AND fund college — the money won't stretch, but the carpentry, the backyard and the tool library might.
c11_hs_ch10.goal: Distinguish money, real and psychic income and apply budgeting as a goal-driven plan.

discovery.question: Fresh blood on a silk scarf — first step: soak it in hot water to loosen the stain?
options: Never — heat coagulates the protein and fixes it permanently; cold water only, and silk won't tolerate alkalis
Yes — hot water dissolves stains fastest
Yes — then add chlorine bleach
Never — silk must go straight to dry-cleaning regardless
discovery.answer: Never — heat coagulates the protein and fixes it permanently; cold water only, and silk won't tolerate alkalis
discovery.hook: And mend before you wash — the machine's agitation turns a 2 cm tear into a 10 cm rip; laundering is the amplifier, not the cure.

c11_hs_ch11.mission: Decode a care label's four symbols — 40°C tub, crossed 'CL' triangle, one-dot dryer, two-dot iron — then choose the right first aid for turmeric on cotton and blood on silk.
c11_hs_ch11.finale: Care isn't washing — it's five disciplines (mending, laundry, stain removal, finishing, storage) each dictated by the fibre's chemistry.
c11_hs_ch11.subtitle: Read the tiny symbols before the washing machine reads them for you.
c11_hs_ch11.intro: A red kurta fades and a silk dupatta shrinks in one wash — the care label knew; nobody read it.
c11_hs_ch11.goal: Apply fibre properties to laundering, stain removal and mending decisions.

discovery.question: 'A smartphone isn't a computer system — no separate CPU, keyboard or monitor.' True?
options: False — the SoC carries CPU and memory, the touchscreen is input and output, and an OS runs the apps; the shape differs, the architecture doesn't
True — computers need a cabinet and keyboard
True — phones only run apps, not programs
False — but only because phones have cameras
discovery.answer: False — the SoC carries CPU and memory, the touchscreen is input and output, and an OS runs the apps; the shape differs, the architecture doesn't
discovery.hook: And the CPU isn't the computer either — it's one organ in a system of input, process, storage and output, like a scanner beeping a library book in.

c11_ip_ch01.mission: Map a barcode-scanner book issue onto input-process-output, then choose between a fast-CPU/8GB and slow-CPU/32GB laptop for a 20GB dataset.
c11_ip_ch01.finale: A fast brain with a tiny desk loses to a slower brain with a big one — RAM is where the data must sit while the CPU works.
c11_ip_ch01.subtitle: Prove a phone is a computer — and that the CPU isn't one.
c11_ip_ch01.role: a buyer decoding a spec sheet honestly
c11_ip_ch01.intro: i5, 16GB, SSD, Windows, Office — which lines are hardware you can touch and which are code that makes the touchable parts work?
c11_ip_ch01.goal: Define a computer system and separate hardware, system software and application software.

discovery.question: A script written on a Windows laptop runs unmodified on the lab's Linux machines. Which Python feature made that trip possible?
options: Cross-platform portability — each OS has its own interpreter, and modules like os.path abstract the differences
Compiled binaries — Windows secretly built a Linux version
The code avoided all operating-system calls
Luck — it just happened to work
discovery.answer: Cross-platform portability — each OS has its own interpreter, and modules like os.path abstract the differences
discovery.hook: 'Interpreted means too slow for real work' — tell that to NumPy and TensorFlow, whose heavy lifting is C under a Python hood.

c11_ip_ch02.mission: Install Python with 'Add to PATH' ticked, verify with python --version, and judge when IDLE is enough and when a real IDE is owed.
c11_ip_ch02.finale: The interpreter runs your lines the moment you write them — no compile step, no excuses between idea and output.
c11_ip_ch02.subtitle: Get from installer checkbox to running code without the usual potholes.
c11_ip_ch02.role: a first-time Python user making the install actually work
c11_ip_ch02.intro: One unchecked box at install — 'Add Python to PATH' — decides whether the command line knows your language exists.
c11_ip_ch02.goal: Explain Python's interpreted, portable, dynamic design and set up a working environment.

discovery.question: Evaluate in your head: `True or False and False` — what does Python actually compute?
options: True — `and` binds tighter than `or`, so it's `True or (False and False)`
False — left to right gives `True or False` then `and False`
False — `or` always wins over `and`
An error — mixed operators can't combine
discovery.answer: True — `and` binds tighter than `or`, so it's `True or (False and False)`
discovery.hook: And indentation isn't decoration — dedent `print(fact)` one level and it escapes the loop entirely; in Python the whitespace is the syntax.

c11_ip_ch03.mission: Convert 'if score ≥ 50 print Pass and set grade' into correctly indented blocks, then trace a factorial loop to see what escapes the indentation.
c11_ip_ch03.finale: Write `33 <= marks <= 100` — Python reads logic like mathematics, but only if you respect the precedence and the tabs.
c11_ip_ch03.subtitle: Learn that whitespace is grammar and `and` outranks `or`.
c11_ip_ch03.role: a programmer whose bugs live in the left margin
c11_ip_ch03.intro: Directions to a friend: 'go straight, IF the main road's crowded take the service lane' — control flow is just that, typed.
c11_ip_ch03.goal: Use indentation-defined blocks, relational operators and Boolean precedence correctly.

discovery.question: You must store 'ATCGATCG' and later swap the third base for 'G' — string or list?
options: List — strings are immutable so `dna[2] = 'G'` fails; a list mutates in place
String — DNA is text, so text type is correct
Either — both mutate the same way
String — lists can't hold characters
discovery.answer: List — strings are immutable so `dna[2] = 'G'` fails; a list mutates in place
discovery.hook: And `list1 = list2` doesn't copy — it gives one list two names, so 'fixing' list1 silently vandalises list2.

c11_ip_ch04.mission: Build a record list mixing name, ID and a nested marks list, change one field by index, then slice positions 2 to 5 cleanly.
c11_ip_ch04.finale: Ordered, mutable, heterogeneous — the list is Python's general-purpose record; learn where it ends and the string begins.
c11_ip_ch04.subtitle: Pick the container that can actually change its contents.
c11_ip_ch04.role: a data wrangler choosing the right container
c11_ip_ch04.intro: Name, roll number, five subject marks, a percentage — one variable, four types. Only one built-in holds all that.
c11_ip_ch04.goal: Use lists' mutability, indexing and slicing — and know when a string can't do the job.

discovery.question: The program runs without error and prints nothing. The last line reads `calculate` — where's the bug?
options: Missing parentheses — `calculate` only references the function object; `calculate()` is what invokes it
Python refused to run the function silently
The variables a and b went out of scope
The function needs a return statement to print
discovery.answer: Missing parentheses — `calculate` only references the function object; `calculate()` is what invokes it
discovery.hook: And `def` alone never executes anything — definition is a recipe, the call is the cooking; also, functions organise code, they don't speed it up.

c11_ip_ch05.mission: Refactor a 20-shape if-elif into named functions, expose the maintenance and reuse failures of copy-paste, then call print_line() three times correctly.
c11_ip_ch05.finale: Write the logic once, name it, call it anywhere — the function's real payoff is a program you can change without fear.
c11_ip_ch05.subtitle: Catch the call that never happened — and why reuse beats speed as the reason for functions.
c11_ip_ch05.role: a developer shrinking a copy-paste monster
c11_ip_ch05.intro: GST and discount logic rewritten for every canteen order — one rate change and twenty places to fix. There is a better shape.
c11_ip_ch05.goal: Separate function definition from invocation and justify modularity by maintainability, not speed.

discovery.question: A program opens a file, writes data, then crashes before `close()` — is the data safely on disk?
options: Not guaranteed — Python buffers output, and only close() (or flush()) forces the buffer to disk
Yes — the OS saves everything automatically
Yes — write() always hits the disk instantly
No — the file is always left empty
discovery.answer: Not guaranteed — Python buffers output, and only close() (or flush()) forces the buffer to disk
discovery.hook: And open() doesn't read anything — it hands you a handle; the data only moves when you explicitly read or write.

c11_ip_ch06.mission: Split report-card data into CSV text and scanned signatures into binary, then defend why 'always use binary mode' is bad advice for text.
c11_ip_ch06.finale: Every file is bytes underneath; text mode's gift is encoding and newline translation you don't have to manage yourself.
c11_ip_ch06.subtitle: Learn the open-work-close rhythm — and what the buffer hides from you.
c11_ip_ch06.role: a programmer making exam marks survive a restart
c11_ip_ch06.intro: Variables die when the program exits — only a file on disk remembers tomorrow. Open it, do the work, close it.
c11_ip_ch06.goal: Choose text vs binary files correctly and explain open/close and buffering.

discovery.question: A designer argues: allow NULL in RollNumber because a new student may not have one yet. Does the relational model permit it?
options: No — RollNumber is the primary key, and NULL can't equal NULL, so two unassigned students would break tuple uniqueness
Yes — NULL means unknown, which is accurate here
Yes — as long as only one student lacks it
No — primary keys must be letters, not numbers
discovery.answer: No — RollNumber is the primary key, and NULL can't equal NULL, so two unassigned students would break tuple uniqueness
discovery.hook: Two rows can share the same city and country legitimately — tuples are distinct on the whole row, not on any single column.

c11_ip_ch07.mission: Expose why two CSV files can't answer 'Name, Subject, Marks' like a join can, then count a table's degree and cardinality correctly.
c11_ip_ch07.finale: Files scatter, relations link — a DBMS exists so a changed phone number is written once, not hunted through three registers.
c11_ip_ch07.subtitle: Give every part of a table its precise name — and see why NULL can't hold a key.
c11_ip_ch07.role: a database designer digitising a school's registers
c11_ip_ch07.intro: Three paper registers, one changed phone number, three places to update — the relational model was invented for exactly this mess.
c11_ip_ch07.goal: Distinguish relation, tuple, attribute, domain and keys, and contrast DBMS with file systems.

discovery.question: Average marks per subject, plotted as a line chart 'because lines show trends.' Sound choice?
options: No — subjects are categories, not a timeline; comparison wants a bar chart, and the question picks the chart
Yes — lines show trends, always
Yes — any chart fits any data
No — only pie charts show subject marks
discovery.answer: No — subjects are categories, not a timeline; comparison wants a bar chart, and the question picks the chart
discovery.hook: There's no single 'correct' chart — monthly sales want a line for trend, a bar for month-vs-month; the data is fixed but the question chooses.

c11_ip_ch08.mission: Pick box plot over bar to compare mark distributions across streams, then draw a 7-day temperature line with plt.plot — and remember what actually renders it.
c11_ip_ch08.finale: plt.plot() only prepares the drawing; plt.show() is what puts it on screen — the picture exists in memory first, always.
c11_ip_ch08.subtitle: Match the chart to the question — and the show() to the plot.
c11_ip_ch08.role: an analyst turning 110 raw numbers into one insight
c11_ip_ch08.intro: Ten matches, eleven batsmen, a spreadsheet of runs — the eye can't read it; the right chart can.
c11_ip_ch08.goal: Select visualisations by analytical task and produce basic Matplotlib plots correctly.

discovery.question: The set of all lines parallel to the x-axis — finite, since you can only draw so many on a page?
options: Infinite — every real number c gives a distinct line y = c; the pencil's limits aren't the mathematics' limits
Finite — a sheet holds only so many lines
Finite — parallel lines all coincide anyway
Infinite — because the x-axis itself is infinitely long
discovery.answer: Infinite — every real number c gives a distinct line y = c; the pencil's limits aren't the mathematics' limits
discovery.hook: And {0} is not the empty set — it has one element (zero); {φ} is a singleton holding the empty set. Small braces, big differences.

c11_math_ch01.mission: Classify {x² ≤ 4 over ℤ}, {x² = −1 over ℝ} and {multiples of 7} into empty, finite or infinite — then flip between roster and set-builder fluently.
c11_math_ch01.finale: A set answers one question — is this in or out? If 'yes' and 'no' can't be decided objectively, the collection isn't a set at all.
c11_math_ch01.subtitle: Learn why 'well-defined' is the whole definition — and why {0} is never empty.
c11_math_ch01.role: a set-builder separating the countable from the uncountable
c11_math_ch01.intro: 'Students above 90%' is a set; 'talented students' is not — the difference is whether membership can be decided at all.
c11_math_ch01.goal: Apply the well-defined criterion, distinct elements, and the empty/finite/infinite classification.

discovery.question: A = {1, 2}, B = {3, 4}. Both A × B and B × A have four pairs — so they're equal?
options: No — pairs are ordered; (1, 3) and (3, 1) are different objects, so the products differ
Yes — sets don't care about order
Yes — cardinality equality is set equality
No — because 1 isn't in B
discovery.answer: No — pairs are ordered; (1, 3) and (3, 1) are different objects, so the products differ
discovery.hook: The outer set is unordered, but each pair inside has a fixed first and second seat — (subject, teacher) is not (teacher, subject).

c11_math_ch02.mission: List P × Q for small sets, recover A and B from a given product, and verify the distributive law A × (B ∪ C) by hand.
c11_math_ch02.finale: n(A × B) = n(A) × n(B) — multiplication, not addition; the product is a grid of pairs, not a merger of sets.
c11_math_ch02.subtitle: Pair sets carefully — order inside the brackets is the whole meaning.
c11_math_ch02.role: a timetable designer pairing subjects with slots
c11_math_ch02.intro: Three subjects, two teachers — how many assignments? The Cartesian product is the systematic way to count and name them all.
c11_math_ch02.goal: Compute Cartesian products, respect ordered pairs, and use the cardinality and distributive rules.

discovery.question: A wheel of radius 0.5 m turns through 120°. Distance travelled by a rim point: 0.5 × 120 = 60 m?
options: No — l = rθ only works in radians: convert 120° to 2π/3, giving π/3 m ≈ 1.05 m
Yes — multiply radius by the angle
Yes — but convert to 60 km
No — the answer is 0.5 × 360 = 180 m
discovery.answer: No — l = rθ only works in radians: convert 120° to 2π/3, giving π/3 m ≈ 1.05 m
discovery.hook: A radian is a pure ratio — arc over radius — which is why calculus and physics refuse to work in degrees.

c11_math_ch03.mission: Convert 22°30′ into an exact multiple of π, then judge whether 'multiply by 57.3' is ever acceptable for exact answers.
c11_math_ch03.finale: Degrees × π/180 = radians; radians × 180/π = degrees — get the direction wrong and 90° becomes 16,200/π.
c11_math_ch03.subtitle: Convert between degrees and radians without flipping the fraction.
c11_math_ch03.role: a ride designer translating a safety limit into controller units
c11_math_ch03.intro: A Ferris wheel spins three times a minute — the operator says 1080°, the physics wants radians per second; one ratio bridges them.
c11_math_ch03.goal: Convert degrees↔radians exactly and apply l = rθ only in radian measure.

discovery.question: Induction 'proves' all horses share one colour: true for 1 horse; removing different horses always leaves same-coloured sets. Where does it break?
options: At k = 1 → k = 2 — the two reduced sets share no horse, so the colour can't transfer between them
At the base case — one horse can be two colours
At the hypothesis — induction never works on animals
Nowhere — the proof is correct
discovery.answer: At k = 1 → k = 2 — the two reduced sets share no horse, so the colour can't transfer between them
discovery.hook: And 'assume P(k) is true for all k' is circular — the hypothesis is one arbitrary, fixed k; the domino only needs to fall once per step.

c11_math_ch04.mission: Anchor a base case at the right starting value (2ⁿ > n² begins at n = 5, not n = 1), then drive P(k) → P(k+1) without assuming the conclusion.
c11_math_ch04.finale: Prove step one exists and that every step hands off to the next — the infinite staircase is then climbed without climbing.
c11_math_ch04.subtitle: Learn the two dominoes of induction — and the one faulty step that fakes a proof.
c11_math_ch04.role: a prover checking whether a staircase can be climbed forever
c11_math_ch04.intro: You don't verify 1+3+5+...=n² for every n — you verify the first tile stands and that each tile tips the next.
c11_math_ch04.goal: Execute the base case and inductive step correctly and spot invalid induction arguments.

discovery.question: √(−4) × √(−9) = √36 = 6 — quick check, right?
options: Wrong — (2i)(3i) = 6i² = −6; the product rule for roots only survives for non-negative radicands
Right — roots multiply under one radical
Right — the negatives cancel
Wrong — the answer is 6i, not −6
discovery.answer: Wrong — (2i)(3i) = 6i² = −6; the product rule for roots only survives for non-negative radicands
discovery.hook: The imaginary part of 2 − 5i is −5, a real number — i is not a variable to cancel, and Im(z) never carries the i.

c11_math_ch05.mission: Solve x² + 9 = 0 with ±3i, put (2 + √−16)/2 into a + ib form, and argue whether 'no real roots' ever meant 'no roots.'
c11_math_ch05.finale: Every extension of the number system was once 'impossible' — negatives for x + 5 = 3, fractions for 3x = 1, i for x² = −1.
c11_math_ch05.subtitle: Meet the number invented to keep equations solvable — and the rule it quietly breaks.
c11_math_ch05.role: a mathematician extending the number line into a plane
c11_math_ch05.intro: A spring equation ends at x² = −9 and the real numbers surrender — so mathematics grew a new dimension rather than accept defeat.
c11_math_ch05.goal: Compute with i correctly, respect the restricted radical rule, and read real/imaginary parts precisely.

discovery.question: Solving −4x + 12 ≤ 20: −4x ≤ 8, so x ≤ −2. Sound?
options: No — dividing by −4 reverses the sign: x ≥ −2, the opposite ray entirely
Yes — the algebra is identical to equations
Yes — the solution is (−∞, −2]
No — the answer should be x ≤ 2
discovery.answer: No — dividing by −4 reverses the sign: x ≥ −2, the opposite ray entirely
discovery.hook: 2 < 5 but −2 > −5 — multiplying by a negative mirrors the number line, so the inequality must turn around with it.

c11_math_ch06.mission: Solve (2x − 7)/3 ≥ (x + 5)/2 − 1 to x ≥ 23, then draw the solution ray with the right circle — closed for ≤, open for <.
c11_math_ch06.finale: Equations give a point; inequalities give a ray — and the ray points the other way the moment a negative divides.
c11_math_ch06.subtitle: Catch the flip that turns a whole solution set inside out.
c11_math_ch06.role: a budgeter turning constraints into intervals
c11_math_ch06.intro: ₹500, notebooks at ₹45, keep ₹50 for the bus — the answer isn't a number, it's a range, and one wrong sign erases it.
c11_math_ch06.goal: Solve linear inequalities with correct sign reversal and represent solutions on the number line.

discovery.question: Three-digit numbers from digits 1–5, no repetition: 5 choices × 5 × 5 = 125?
options: No — each used digit is gone: 5 × 4 × 3 = 60
Yes — three positions, five digits each
Yes — repetition doesn't change the count
discovery.answer: No — each used digit is gone: 5 × 4 × 3 = 60
discovery.hook: And 10!/8! is not (10/8)! — the factorial is a function, not a factor: it unwraps to 10 × 9 = 90.

c11_math_ch07.mission: Count a 4×5×3 complete meal, then verify the constraint-first method: fix the even units digit, then count the rest.
c11_math_ch07.finale: Multiply only when choices are independent — when a choice spends a digit, the next multiplication must shrink with it.
c11_math_ch07.subtitle: Learn when choices multiply — and when they shrink each other.
c11_math_ch07.role: a counter who multiplies instead of listing
c11_math_ch07.intro: Three shirts, two trousers — six outfits without listing one. Scale it to digits and the independence question bites.
c11_math_ch07.goal: Apply the multiplication principle correctly to dependent and independent choices, and manipulate factorials.

discovery.question: In (x² + 1/x)¹², a student says the x-free term sits at r = 4. Check the exponent.
options: Wrong — the term's power is 24 − 3r, so the constant needs r = 8
Right — r = 4 balances the powers
Right — 12/3 = 4 always gives the middle
Wrong — no constant term exists in this expansion
discovery.answer: Wrong — the term's power is 24 − 3r, so the constant needs r = 8
discovery.hook: And the fifth term uses r = 4, not r = 5 — T_{r+1} is off-by-one by design, and the minus sign in (−2/x) is raised to r too.

c11_math_ch08.mission: Expand (2x − 3y)⁴ coefficient by coefficient, then extract exactly the fifth term of (3x² − 2/x)⁷ without writing the rest.
c11_math_ch08.finale: Powers of a fall while powers of b climb, always summing to n — the general term is a slot machine you can read directly.
c11_math_ch08.subtitle: Read a binomial expansion by its address, not by multiplying it out.
c11_math_ch08.role: an accountant shortcutting (100 + 2)⁵ for compound interest
c11_math_ch08.intro: (a + b)¹⁵ has sixteen terms — but the formula hands you the eighth alone, no multiplication marathon required.
c11_math_ch08.goal: Use the general term T_{r+1} with correct indexing, signs and exponents.

discovery.question: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25 — the differences 3, 5, 7, 9 form a pattern, so the sequence is arithmetic?
options: No — arithmetic demands a constant difference; patterned differences mean this is the sequence of squares
Yes — any patterned difference makes it arithmetic
Yes — it increases steadily
No — it's geometric with ratio 3
discovery.answer: No — arithmetic demands a constant difference; patterned differences mean this is the sequence of squares
discovery.hook: And the nth term of an AP is a + (n − 1)d — the first term has had zero additions of d, which is why 'a + nd' overshoots by exactly one.

c11_math_ch09.mission: Check ratios on 3, 6, 12, 24 to name it geometric, then recover a and d from '5th term 22, 9th term 38' without the off-by-one.
c11_math_ch09.finale: Constant difference → AP, constant ratio → GP, patterned difference → look again; the test must match the definition.
c11_math_ch09.subtitle: Test the pattern before trusting it — and add d exactly n − 1 times.
c11_math_ch09.role: a saver tracking deposits that grow by rule
c11_math_ch09.intro: ₹500 this month, ₹600 next, ₹700 after — the formula that predicts December without adding eleven times is the point.
c11_math_ch09.goal: Classify sequences by difference and ratio, and apply aₙ = a + (n − 1)d precisely.

discovery.question: Where does the point (0, −5) lie — fourth quadrant, since its y is negative?
options: Nowhere in a quadrant — it sits on the negative y-axis; quadrants need both coordinates non-zero
Fourth quadrant — negative y decides it
Third quadrant — negatives mean III
Second quadrant — axes count as quadrants
discovery.answer: Nowhere in a quadrant — it sits on the negative y-axis; quadrants need both coordinates non-zero
discovery.hook: Axes are the borders, not the countries — and (3, 2) is not (2, 3); the ordered pair's order is the point's whole identity.

c11_math_ch10.mission: Plot A(2,3), B(−2,3), C(−2,−3), D(2,−3) to see the square, then find the x-axis point equidistant from (2,3) and (4,5).
c11_math_ch10.finale: Distance is just Pythagoras on a grid — horizontal leg, vertical leg, hypotenuse — no special case for points on axes.
c11_math_ch10.subtitle: Learn that a point on an axis belongs to no quadrant at all.
c11_math_ch10.role: a navigator reading signed distances from two axes
c11_math_ch10.intro: Cinema seat = row plus seat number; a plane point = x then y — and the border seats belong to no quadrant.
c11_math_ch10.goal: Plot points, classify quadrants and axes, and apply the distance formula.

discovery.question: Slice a double cone with a plane parallel to its base — out comes a parabola, right?
options: No — parallel to the base means perpendicular to the axis, which cuts a circle; the parabola needs the plane parallel to a generator
Yes — parallel slices give parabolas
Yes — anything between circle and hyperbola is parabola
No — that cut gives a hyperbola
discovery.answer: No — parallel to the base means perpendicular to the axis, which cuts a circle; the parabola needs the plane parallel to a generator
discovery.hook: And (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r² is only a circle while r > 0 — r = 0 is a single point, r < 0 is no curve at all.

c11_math_ch11.mission: Decide the conic when a plane meets the axis at 30° while the generator sits at 45°, then complete the square on x² + y² − 6x + 8y = 0.
c11_math_ch11.finale: Circle, ellipse, parabola, hyperbola — one cone, one tilt of the knife, four different curves.
c11_math_ch11.subtitle: Watch one tilted plane generate four different curves.
c11_math_ch11.role: a dish designer choosing the cross-section that focuses signal
c11_math_ch11.intro: A satellite dish must bounce every signal to one focus — which is why its profile is a parabola, and why the slice angle matters.
c11_math_ch11.goal: Classify conics by the plane's angle to the axis and read circle equations by completing the square.

discovery.question: Distance from the origin to (1, 1, 1)? Easy — 1 + 1 + 1 = 3.
options: No — Euclidean distance squares first: √(1² + 1² + 1²) = √3; adding differences gives a taxicab metric, not length
Yes — coordinates sum to the distance
Yes — and in 2D it'd be x + y
No — it's exactly 1
discovery.answer: No — Euclidean distance squares first: √(1² + 1² + 1²) = √3; adding differences gives a taxicab metric, not length
discovery.hook: And (0, 0, −4) is on the z-axis but NOT in the XY-plane — an axis needs two zero coordinates, a plane needs its own missing one.

c11_math_ch12.mission: Drop a perpendicular from (2, −3, 6) to the XY-plane correctly, then compute the 3D distance between (2, −1, 3) and (−4, 5, −2).
c11_math_ch12.finale: The third coordinate is just one more leg in Pythagoras — base diagonal, then space diagonal.
c11_math_ch12.subtitle: Add one axis — and learn that summing isn't measuring.
c11_math_ch12.role: an architect locating a light fixture in a room's volume
c11_math_ch12.intro: A floor plan finds the wall distances; a third number — height — turns a map into a building.
c11_math_ch12.goal: Locate points in octants and on planes, and apply the 3D distance formula.

discovery.question: lim (x² − 4)/(x − 2) as x → 2: substitute and get 0/0 = 0 — settled?
options: No — 0/0 is indeterminate, a signal to factor: (x−2)(x+2)/(x−2) = x+2 → 4
Yes — zero over zero is zero
No — the limit doesn't exist because f(2) is undefined
Yes — direct substitution always gives the limit
discovery.answer: No — 0/0 is indeterminate, a signal to factor: (x−2)(x+2)/(x−2) = x+2 → 4
discovery.hook: The limit asks what the function tends toward, not what it equals — a car doing 60 up to the booth still tends to 60 even if it stops there.

c11_math_ch13.mission: Build a two-sided table for |x|/x at 0 to prove the limit fails, then evaluate (x³−1)/(x²−1) by cancelling the common factor.
c11_math_ch13.finale: Left and right limits must agree — |x|/x approaches −1 and +1 simultaneously, so no limit exists at zero.
c11_math_ch13.subtitle: Learn that 0/0 is a question, not an answer.
c11_math_ch13.role: an analyst finding what a function approaches, not what it says
c11_math_ch13.intro: The speedometer reads 60 until the booth — the value AT the booth doesn't decide what speed the car was tending to.
c11_math_ch13.goal: Evaluate limits via factorisation and recognise indeterminate forms and one-sided disagreement.

discovery.question: 'All prime numbers are odd' — is it even a mathematical statement, given that it's false?
options: Yes — a statement is anything with a definite truth value; false ones count, and its negation is 'some prime is not odd'
No — only true sentences are statements
No — it contains a category error
Yes — but its negation is 'all primes are even'
discovery.answer: Yes — a statement is anything with a definite truth value; false ones count, and its negation is 'some prime is not odd'
discovery.hook: 'x > 5' isn't a statement, but 'for all real x, x > 5' is — the quantifier binds the variable and the sentence gets a verdict: false.

c11_math_ch14.mission: Sort commands, open sentences and claims into statement-or-not, then negate 'x is even and x > 10' without forgetting to flip the 'and.'
c11_math_ch14.finale: Negate 'some are' with 'none are'; negate 'all are' with 'some aren't' — the quantifier flips before the predicate does.
c11_math_ch14.subtitle: Learn that a false sentence is still a statement — and how to negate one honestly.
c11_math_ch14.role: a logician checking whether sentences carry a truth value
c11_math_ch14.intro: 'Solve 2x + 3 = 7' is a command; 'π is rational' is a statement — one has a truth value, the other never could.
c11_math_ch14.goal: Identify mathematical statements and form correct negations across quantifiers and connectives.

discovery.question: Force = mass × acceleration, so the unit of force is kg·m/s — correct?
options: No — acceleration is m/s², so the newton unfolds as kg·m·s⁻²; kg·m/s is momentum's unit
Yes — velocity and acceleration share units
Yes — newton is a fundamental unit anyway
No — it's kg·m·s⁻¹
discovery.answer: No — acceleration is m/s², so the newton unfolds as kg·m·s⁻²; kg·m/s is momentum's unit
discovery.hook: Newtons and joules aren't fundamental — they're shorthand; every derived unit is base units multiplied and divided with no hidden factor.

c11_phy_ch01.mission: Convert 72 km/h into 20 m/s honestly, then break 'J·s' and 'N' back into base units until nothing but m, kg, s remains.
c11_phy_ch01.finale: A measurement is a number times a standard — lose the unit and '5' could mean five grams or five tonnes.
c11_phy_ch01.subtitle: Unpack the famous units into the seven base ones underneath.
c11_phy_ch01.role: a lab calibrator checking what a unit really contains
c11_phy_ch01.intro: The dairy's steel 'litre' and NPL's light-speed-defined metre are the same word with very different pedigrees.
c11_phy_ch01.goal: Distinguish base from derived units and express any unit in SI base form.

discovery.question: Walk 2 km at 4 km/h, then 2 km at 6 km/h — average speed is (4+6)/2 = 5 km/h?
options: No — equal distances mean more time is spent slow: total 4 km over 5/6 h gives 4.8 km/h
Yes — average speed is the mean of speeds
Yes — arithmetic mean always applies
No — the answer is 6 km/h
discovery.answer: No — equal distances mean more time is spent slow: total 4 km over 5/6 h gives 4.8 km/h
discovery.hook: And a round trip has zero average velocity but positive average speed — displacement and path length are not the same animal.

c11_phy_ch02.mission: For a cyclist going −10 m → +20 m → −5 m, compute path length (55 m), displacement (+5 m) and see how far apart they sit.
c11_phy_ch02.finale: The arithmetic mean only works when the clock ticks equally — average by time, not by speed.
c11_phy_ch02.subtitle: Learn why a round trip's velocity is zero while its speed never was.
c11_phy_ch02.role: a race analyst splitting distance from displacement
c11_phy_ch02.intro: The Metro goes out 5 km and comes back 5 km — one quantity reports ten kilometres, the other reports zero.
c11_phy_ch02.goal: Distinguish path length from displacement and compute average speed by total distance over total time.

discovery.question: After one complete lap of a circular track of radius R, the displacement is 2πR — true?
options: No — start and finish coincide, so displacement is zero; 2πR is the path length
Yes — the circumference is the displacement
Yes — vectors add along the curve
No — it's R, the radius
discovery.answer: No — start and finish coincide, so displacement is zero; 2πR is the path length
discovery.hook: Having units doesn't make a quantity scalar and having a number doesn't — direction is the independent credential a vector must carry.

c11_phy_ch03.mission: Add 30 m at 30° to 40 m at 60° head-to-tail on paper, then explain why triangle and parallelogram must give the same resultant.
c11_phy_ch03.finale: A vector is free — slide it parallel to itself and it stays the same vector; that's why the two drawing methods can never disagree.
c11_phy_ch03.subtitle: See why a full lap's displacement vanishes while its distance doesn't.
c11_phy_ch03.role: a navigator adding journeys that don't add like numbers
c11_phy_ch03.intro: A boat aims straight across a river and lands downstream — two velocities conspired, and only vector addition explains where.
c11_phy_ch03.goal: Separate scalars from vectors and add vectors graphically with confidence in the result.

discovery.question: 'Stop pedalling and my bicycle stops — so Galileo was wrong and motion does need force.' Evaluate.
options: Observation right, conclusion wrong — friction is the net force; the pedal force was only ever cancelling it
Completely right — Aristotle stands
Completely wrong — bicycles don't stop
Right — because road contact is a force
discovery.answer: Observation right, conclusion wrong — friction is the net force; the pedal force was only ever cancelling it
discovery.hook: Inertia isn't a force keeping things moving — it's the property that makes a force necessary to change velocity at all.

c11_phy_ch04.mission: Run Galileo's double incline to its flat conclusion — same height, then infinite distance — then find the friction on a box pushed steadily at 2 m/s.
c11_phy_ch04.finale: A car cruising at constant 60 has engine thrust exactly balancing drag — net force zero, motion sustained; force changes motion, it doesn't keep it.
c11_phy_ch04.subtitle: Unmask the hidden force that made Aristotle's fallacy feel true.
c11_phy_ch04.role: a Galileo rerunning the incline in thought
c11_phy_ch04.intro: A marble on carpet stops, on smooth floor rolls far, on frictionless ice — never. Removing the confounder was the whole insight.
c11_phy_ch04.goal: State the first law as net-force-zero and distinguish inertia from a force.

discovery.question: You push a wall with all your strength and it doesn't budge — how much work did you do on the wall?
options: Zero — no displacement means W = F·d·cosθ = 0; the effort you feel is your muscles spending energy, not work on the wall
A lot — big force means big work
Negative — the wall pushed back
Equal to your fatigue in joules
discovery.answer: Zero — no displacement means W = F·d·cosθ = 0; the effort you feel is your muscles spending energy, not work on the wall
discovery.hook: And when force varies, the final force times distance is wrong — the work is the area under the F–x curve, an integral.

c11_phy_ch05.mission: Dot (3i + 4j) N with (2i − j) m to get 2 J, then integrate F = 5x + 2 from 0 to 4 and hand 48 J to the work-energy theorem.
c11_phy_ch05.finale: Only the force's component along the displacement earns its keep — a coolie's upward force does no work on a suitcase walking sideways.
c11_phy_ch05.subtitle: Learn that effort and work are different currencies.
c11_phy_ch05.role: a physicist billing forces only for displaced metres
c11_phy_ch05.intro: The coolie sweats under a suitcase and physics pays him zero joules — the angle between force and motion is everything.
c11_phy_ch05.goal: Compute work via the dot product, its sign, and integration for variable forces.

discovery.question: A Diwali rocket explodes mid-flight into a hundred fragments — where does the centre of mass go?
options: It keeps tracing the original parabola — internal forces cancel in pairs; only external gravity steers the CM
It falls straight down once the pieces scatter
It speeds up from the explosion's energy
It stops — the system no longer exists
discovery.answer: It keeps tracing the original parabola — internal forces cancel in pairs; only external gravity steers the CM
discovery.hook: A uniform ring's centre of mass sits at its geometric centre — a point containing zero mass; the CM needn't live inside the material at all.

c11_phy_ch06.mission: Find the CM of an L-shaped lamina of three unit squares, then argue why the exploding bomb's fragments can't move their shared centre.
c11_phy_ch06.finale: Fragments fly every direction; the mass-weighted average keeps falling like nothing happened — internal chaos can't bend an external path.
c11_phy_ch06.subtitle: Watch a hundred fragments obey one invisible point.
c11_phy_ch06.role: a tracker following a point with no mass in it
c11_phy_ch06.intro: Each blade particle of a fan circles differently, yet the fan 'as a whole' moves simply — that average point does all the bookkeeping.
c11_phy_ch06.goal: Compute centre of mass and explain why internal forces can't deflect its motion.

discovery.question: Two 1 kg masses at 1 m pull each other with 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N. Double the distance — the force halves?
options: No — gravity is inverse-square: twice the distance means one quarter the force, 1.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N
Yes — force shrinks linearly with distance
Yes — 3.33 × 10⁻¹¹ N
No — it drops to zero beyond a metre
discovery.answer: No — gravity is inverse-square: twice the distance means one quarter the force, 1.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N
discovery.hook: And the Sun is not at the centre of the ellipse — it sits at a focus; symmetry of the orbit is not symmetry of the pull.

c11_phy_ch07.mission: Test Kepler's second law against a 'symmetric halves take equal time' claim, then judge whether two students on a bench really do attract each other.
c11_phy_ch07.finale: The Moon's acceleration is g/3600 — matching the distance ratio squared; Newton unified the falling apple and the unfalling Moon with one law.
c11_phy_ch07.subtitle: Halve the guess, quarter the force — gravity squares, not halves.
c11_phy_ch07.role: an astronomer checking Newton's inverse-square arithmetic
c11_phy_ch07.intro: The apple falls and the Moon doesn't — yet the same pull, weakened 3600-fold over 60 Earth-radii, explains both.
c11_phy_ch07.goal: Apply the inverse-square law and Kepler's laws correctly, distinguishing G from g.

discovery.question: 'Strain is dimensionless, so it's just a mathematical ratio with no physical meaning.' Fair?
options: No — the fractional change decides bending, stretching and failure; dimensionless doesn't mean inconsequential
Yes — no units means no physics
Yes — it's bookkeeping only
No — because strain actually has units of mm
discovery.answer: No — the fractional change decides bending, stretching and failure; dimensionless doesn't mean inconsequential
discovery.hook: Stress isn't a vector wearing a force's clothes — it's defined relative to a surface's orientation, and it isn't interchangeable with pressure.

c11_phy_ch08.mission: Tell tensile, shearing and hydraulic stress apart with a spring, a book-slide and a sunk balloon, then compute a real strain as ΔL/L.
c11_phy_ch08.finale: ΔL alone lies — 1 mm of stretch is trivial for a rope and catastrophic for a hair; the ratio to the original is what matters.
c11_phy_ch08.subtitle: Measure deformation in fractions, not millimetres.
c11_phy_ch08.role: an engineer reading what a rubber band is really saying
c11_phy_ch08.intro: The band stretches 0.5 cm on 10 cm — that 5% number, not the millimetres, is what the material actually feels.
c11_phy_ch08.goal: Define stress relative to surface orientation and strain as fractional deformation.

discovery.question: A hydraulic press: 50 N on 2 cm² lifts 5000 N on 200 cm². So keep enlarging the piston and lift anything for free?
options: No — pressure transmits equally but energy doesn't multiply; the big piston rises only a fraction as far
Yes — area ratio is free force
Yes — Pascal's law guarantees it
No — fluid pressure has a maximum of 1 atm
discovery.answer: No — pressure transmits equally but energy doesn't multiply; the big piston rises only a fraction as far
discovery.hook: Pressure has no direction — the force it exerts is normal to the wall, but pressure itself is a scalar at a point, and 'same pressure' only holds at the same depth.

c11_phy_ch09.mission: Push a drawing pin to feel force-per-area, verify 76 cm Hg against 1.013 × 10⁵ Pa, then expose the free-lunch flaw in the ever-bigger piston.
c11_phy_ch09.finale: F₁/A₁ = F₂/A₂ buys force with distance — the small piston travels far so the big one barely moves; no energy is created.
c11_phy_ch09.subtitle: Discover that the hydraulic lift trades distance for force, not energy for nothing.
c11_phy_ch09.role: a mechanic questioning a too-good force multiplier
c11_phy_ch09.intro: One thumb on a narrow piston lifts a 1500 kg car — the fluid transmitted pressure, but it kept the energy ledger balanced.
c11_phy_ch09.goal: Define fluid pressure as scalar, apply Pascal's law, and spot the energy limit on force multiplication.

discovery.question: 'How much heat is contained in 1 kg of water at 100 °C?' — reach for Q = mcΔT?
options: The question is broken — heat is energy in transit, not stored content; you can only ask how much flows for a given temperature drop
Yes — mcΔT gives the heat inside
Yes — 420 kJ is the answer
No — because water can't hold heat at 100 °C
discovery.answer: The question is broken — heat is energy in transit, not stored content; you can only ask how much flows for a given temperature drop
discovery.hook: A 10 °C rise is an 18 °F rise, not 50 — the +32 belongs to the zero-point offset, not to differences; but ΔT in °C and K are identical.

c11_phy_ch10.mission: Explain why the steel spoon burns faster than the wooden one at the same temperature, then correct 'heat flows until both have equal heat.'
c11_phy_ch10.finale: Heat flows until temperatures match — not until 'heat amounts' match; equilibrium is a temperature, never a shared quantity of heat.
c11_phy_ch10.subtitle: Separate the energy in transit from the temperature that drives it.
c11_phy_ch10.role: a calorimetrist refusing to count stored heat
c11_phy_ch10.intro: Two spoons in the same tea, one burns your fingers — temperature set the direction, but the material set the flow.
c11_phy_ch10.goal: Distinguish heat from temperature and handle scale conversions for values versus differences.

discovery.question: 'The human body is an isolated system — it holds a steady 37 °C.' Sound classification?
options: No — it eats, breathes, sweats and radiates: an open system whose constant temperature is active regulation, not isolation
Yes — constant temperature means no exchange
Yes — skin is a sealed boundary
No — it's a closed system, which means isolated
discovery.answer: No — it eats, breathes, sweats and radiates: an open system whose constant temperature is active regulation, not isolation
discovery.hook: And the Zeroth Law isn't a triviality — it makes 'same temperature' well-defined, which is the only reason a thermometer means anything.

c11_phy_ch11.mission: Sort a gas expanding into vacuum, a thermos and the human body into open/closed/isolated, then defend why thermal equilibrium needs a stated law.
c11_phy_ch11.finale: A closed system swaps energy, an open one swaps matter too, an isolated one swaps nothing — the boundary is often imaginary but the classification is not.
c11_phy_ch11.subtitle: Learn that a steady temperature can mean bustling exchange, not isolation.
c11_phy_ch11.intro: Is a sealed lunchbox closed? Is your body? The answer depends on what crosses a boundary you get to choose.
c11_phy_ch11.goal: Classify thermodynamic systems and justify the Zeroth Law as the foundation of temperature.

discovery.question: Newton's √(P/ρ) predicts sound at 280 m/s but measurement says 331 m/s — so the formula is wrong?
options: Not wrong, incomplete — he assumed isothermal compression; Laplace's adiabatic correction √γ fixes it to ~331 m/s
Yes — discard it
Yes — molecules don't collide
No — the experiment was wrong
discovery.answer: Not wrong, incomplete — he assumed isothermal compression; Laplace's adiabatic correction √γ fixes it to ~331 m/s
discovery.hook: 'Random motion' isn't chaos between collisions — each molecule flies in a deterministic straight line; only the initial positions and velocities are random.

c11_phy_ch12.mission: Find the three errors in 'pressure = 2mnv²' — the missing 1/3, the collision rate, the direction — and judge whether elastic collisions mean a gas can never cool.
c11_phy_ch12.finale: Pressure isn't a steady molecular wind — it's the drumbeat of discrete collisions, each delivering 2mv of momentum.
c11_phy_ch12.subtitle: Rebuild the gas-pressure derivation — and rescue Newton's nearly-right formula.
c11_phy_ch12.role: a kinetic theorist averaging a billion collisions
c11_phy_ch12.intro: Each molecule obeys Newton between collisions — the gas's randomness lives in the statistics, not in broken mechanics.
c11_phy_ch12.goal: Derive pressure from molecular collisions and correct Newton's isothermal sound-speed error.

discovery.question: A ceiling fan rotates forever and a ball bounces repeatedly — both repeat, so both are SHM?
options: Neither — SHM demands a restoring force exactly proportional to displacement, F = −kx; mere repetition isn't enough
Yes — anything periodic is simple harmonic
Yes — repetition is the definition
No — but a bouncing ball counts
discovery.answer: Neither — SHM demands a restoring force exactly proportional to displacement, F = −kx; mere repetition isn't enough
discovery.hook: Even the pendulum only qualifies for small swings — −mgL sin θ is approximately −mgLθ, and that approximation is the whole licence.

c11_phy_ch13.mission: Fix θ(t) = 0.2 sin(5t) written in degrees, then test which motions — fan, bouncing ball, small-angle pendulum — truly earn 'simple harmonic.'
c11_phy_ch13.finale: Periodic means it comes back; simple harmonic means a linear pull sends it back — one is a schedule, the other is a law.
c11_phy_ch13.subtitle: Draw the line between merely repeating and truly harmonic.
c11_phy_ch13.role: a metronome maker checking which motions qualify
c11_phy_ch13.intro: A pendulum ticks, a fan spins, a ball bounces — all repeat, but only one has the linear restoring force that defines SHM.
c11_phy_ch13.goal: Distinguish oscillatory from simple harmonic motion using the F = −kx criterion.

discovery.question: Shake a rope's end up and down; the ripple runs along the rope — 'so this is a longitudinal wave, the motion travels forward.' Right?
options: No — the test is particle motion versus wave travel: the rope moves up-down while the wave runs along it — transverse
Yes — forward travel means longitudinal
Yes — waves on strings are longitudinal
No — it's not a wave at all
discovery.answer: No — the test is particle motion versus wave travel: the rope moves up-down while the wave runs along it — transverse
discovery.hook: We draw sound as a sine curve on paper, yet sound is longitudinal — the picture shows pressure, not sideways jiggle.

c11_phy_ch14.mission: Correct the 'higher frequency means faster wave' belief — the medium sets v, so doubling ν halves λ while speed stays put.
c11_phy_ch14.finale: Tension and mass-per-length set the speed; frequency and amplitude only decide the shape of what travels.
c11_phy_ch14.subtitle: Learn that the drawing is a graph, not a portrait of the motion.
c11_phy_ch14.role: a wave-watcher separating particle dance from wave travel
c11_phy_ch14.intro: The wave slides down the rope while each bit of rope just bobs — direction of travel is not direction of wiggle.
c11_phy_ch14.goal: Classify transverse vs longitudinal correctly and identify the medium as the source of wave speed.

discovery.question: 'Absence makes the heart grow fonder' and 'out of sight, out of mind' — both wise, both proverbs. Which one is psychology?
options: Neither — common sense supplies opposite answers on demand; psychology tests which prediction survives evidence
Both — folk wisdom is psychology
The first — it's more romantic
The second — it's more cynical
discovery.answer: Neither — common sense supplies opposite answers on demand; psychology tests which prediction survives evidence
discovery.hook: Dweck's finding that easy tasks reduced performance persistence is exactly the kind of counterintuitive result proverbs can never produce.

c11_psy_ch01.mission: Take the bystander-in-emergency puzzle and separate a retrospective 'people are selfish' shrug from a testable psychological model.
c11_psy_ch01.finale: Common sense explains everything after the fact and predicts nothing — science earns its name by risking a wrong prediction.
c11_psy_ch01.subtitle: See why two opposite proverbs can both be 'common sense' — and neither is science.
c11_psy_ch01.role: a researcher refusing to accept a proverb as a theory
c11_psy_ch01.intro: 'He's aggressive because he's frustrated' sounds right — which is exactly the problem; so would the opposite explanation.
c11_psy_ch01.goal: Distinguish scientific psychology's testable models from common-sense rationalisation.
