discovery.question: Psychological data means IQ scores and questionnaire answers — everything else is just lab noise?
options: No — demographics, room temperature, heart rate and EEG all count as psychological data inside a study
Yes — only mental measurements qualify
Yes — data must be self-reported
No — but only the EEG counts
discovery.answer: No — demographics, room temperature, heart rate and EEG all count as psychological data inside a study
discovery.hook: And description isn't the unscientific step — a careful, systematic record of behaviour is where prediction and explanation begin.

c11_psy_ch02.mission: Classify a therapist's trial — 50 patients, 60% symptom drop — into the goals of psychology, then judge whether rank data is 'more honest' than scores.
c11_psy_ch02.finale: Ranks say who's ahead but not by how much — an interval gap between 1st and 2nd can hide a canyon or a hair's breadth.
c11_psy_ch02.subtitle: Learn what counts as data when the mind is the subject.
c11_psy_ch02.role: a researcher inventorying every signal a study emits
c11_psy_ch02.intro: A heartbeat trace, a birthday, a warm room — in a psychological study all of it is data, not just the questionnaire.
c11_psy_ch02.goal: Identify psychological data broadly and weigh ordinal versus interval measurement.

discovery.question: 'Development is just growth plus maturation.' Does the formula capture it?
options: No — development is lifelong, multidirectional and plastic, and includes losses alongside gains
Yes — the two processes sum to development
Yes — anything not learned is maturation
No — development ends at adolescence
discovery.answer: No — development is lifelong, multidirectional and plastic, and includes losses alongside gains
discovery.hook: Plasticity isn't unlimited potential — 'plastic' means modifiable within biological limits, not expert-at-anything-at-any-age.

c11_psy_ch03.mission: Weigh whether wisdom gaining while processing speed loses is one process or two, then test 'any skill at any age' against the plasticity clause.
c11_psy_ch03.finale: Old age can mean slower reflexes and better judgement in the same person — development runs both directions at once.
c11_psy_ch03.subtitle: Discover that growing up is only half of developing.
c11_psy_ch03.role: a lifespan scientist tracking gains and losses together
c11_psy_ch03.intro: A behaviour appears untaught — maturation, or quiet learning you never noticed? The distinction changes what development means.
c11_psy_ch03.goal: Apply the life-span view — lifelong, multidirectional, plastic, contextual — to human development.

discovery.question: My absolute threshold for a tone is 0 dB — so anything quieter is completely inaudible to me?
options: No — the threshold is a 50%-detection estimate; neural noise means below-threshold tones are sometimes heard
Yes — a threshold is a hard wall
Yes — 0 dB is silence
No — because 0 dB is actually loud
discovery.answer: No — the threshold is a 50%-detection estimate; neural noise means below-threshold tones are sometimes heard
discovery.hook: Sensation and perception aren't assembly-line stages — your brain's 'this is a face' hypothesis tunes the senses within 100 ms, before you're aware.

c11_psy_ch04.mission: Use Gestalt's 'whole differs from the sum' to dismantle 'perception = sum of sensations,' then explain why thresholds are measured over many trials.
c11_psy_ch04.finale: Perceptual constancy is the proof: a door swinging open stays rectangular in your mind though its retinal image keeps warping.
c11_psy_ch04.subtitle: Find the guesswork hidden inside what you see.
c11_psy_ch04.role: a psychophysicist measuring the edge of detection
c11_psy_ch04.intro: The eye delivers raw signal; the brain delivers a verdict — and the verdict starts editing the signal almost immediately.
c11_psy_ch04.goal: Distinguish sensation from perception and read thresholds as probabilistic, not absolute.

discovery.question: After conditioning, the bell 'becomes food' for Pavlov's dog — a fair summary?
options: No — the bell stays a bell; it gains signal value predicting food, and salivation is a preparatory response, not the food-response moved
Yes — the CS replaces the US
Yes — the dog now thinks bell is edible
No — because dogs can't learn sounds
discovery.answer: No — the bell stays a bell; it gains signal value predicting food, and salivation is a preparatory response, not the food-response moved
discovery.hook: Contiguity isn't enough — present the food before the bell (backward conditioning) and the pairing fails; the signal must predict, not just accompany.

c11_psy_ch05.mission: Separate learning from performance — the crammed-then-forgotten exam answer — and test whether 'relatively permanent' survives forgetting.
c11_psy_ch05.finale: Learning is the underlying change; performance is just its momentary evidence — one can fade while the other looked solid.
c11_psy_ch05.subtitle: Watch a bell stay a bell while quietly becoming a prediction.
c11_psy_ch05.role: a behaviourist timing the signal before the food
c11_psy_ch05.intro: The dog salivates to a sound — not because the sound became food, but because it learned to mean food.
c11_psy_ch05.goal: Explain classical conditioning as signal learning and distinguish learning from performance.

discovery.question: Recite a definition aloud twenty times, feel confident — has it reached long-term memory?
options: Probably not — maintenance rehearsal just cycles it in short-term memory; without semantic, elaborative processing it decays when repetition stops
Yes — repetition always transfers to LTM
Yes — twenty reps is plenty
No — because reading is not memorising at all
discovery.answer: Probably not — maintenance rehearsal just cycles it in short-term memory; without semantic, elaborative processing it decays when repetition stops
discovery.hook: Patient KF kept long-term memory while losing short-term — the stage model survived the exception because parallel routes, not broken sequence, explain it.

c11_psy_ch06.mission: Correct the idea that iconic memory is 'step one of memorising,' then judge whether unattended sensory input is lost forever.
c11_psy_ch06.finale: Sensory memory is a buffer, not a store — raw pixels, not meaning; the memory starts where attention starts.
c11_psy_ch06.subtitle: Learn why confident recitation still goes blank on exam day.
c11_psy_ch06.role: a student upgrading their rehearsal strategy
c11_psy_ch06.intro: Twenty readings, one blank exam — the loop kept the words alive and never once built them a home.
c11_psy_ch06.goal: Distinguish maintenance from elaborative rehearsal and place sensory memory correctly.

discovery.question: 'Thinking is when thoughts come to mind' — daydreaming, worrying, recalling a number all qualify?
options: No — thinking is active, goal-directed manipulation of mental representations; passive mental drift isn't thinking in the psychological sense
Yes — any mental content is thinking
Yes — worrying is thinking about problems
No — only logic counts as thinking
discovery.answer: No — thinking is active, goal-directed manipulation of mental representations; passive mental drift isn't thinking in the psychological sense
discovery.hook: 'I'm a visual thinker, not a verbal one' is a myth — everyone rotates images for one task and runs propositions for another; format follows the task.

c11_psy_ch07.mission: Mark the exam answer 'thinking is a mental process we can't see' against NCERT criteria, then test whether two-word 'telegraphic' speech proves innate syntax.
c11_psy_ch07.finale: Recalling a phone number isn't thinking — reshaping what you know to reach a goal is.
c11_psy_ch07.subtitle: Draw the line between having thoughts and doing thinking.
c11_psy_ch07.role: a cognitive scientist policing the definition
c11_psy_ch07.intro: Your mind wanders all day — but psychology reserves 'thinking' for the moments it works toward something.
c11_psy_ch07.goal: Define thinking as goal-directed manipulation and separate format myths from strategy.

discovery.question: You eat, arousal drops — so the motivational cycle is finished forever?
options: No — it's a loop, not a line: need rebuilds, arousal returns, and the cycle recurs as long as the need can recur
Yes — reduction of arousal ends motivation
Yes — that's why it's called a terminal state
No — because hunger is psychological, not biological
discovery.answer: No — it's a loop, not a line: need rebuilds, arousal returns, and the cycle recurs as long as the need can recur
discovery.hook: And hunger isn't a glucose reflex — cortical signals, attention, stress and culture modulate the same empty stomach into different urgency.

c11_psy_ch08.mission: Rediagram the cycle as a genuine loop, then weigh the claim that arousal-reduction makes all human behaviour selfish.
c11_psy_ch08.finale: The drive reduces, then the need regrows — motivation is a thermostat cycle, not a one-way journey to satisfaction.
c11_psy_ch08.subtitle: Read the motivational cycle as a loop — and hunger as more than a reflex.
c11_psy_ch08.role: a psychologist tracking a need that keeps coming back
c11_psy_ch08.intro: Low blood sugar, a favourite smell, a skipped lunch, a festival fast — the same body state produces wildly different hunger.
c11_psy_ch08.goal: Model motivation as a recurring cycle and explain biological motives' cortical and cultural modulation.

discovery.question: A family dividing chores, a class picking a picnic spot, residents fixing maintenance fees — is any of this 'politics'?
options: All of it — collective decision-making under scarcity with binding outcomes is politics, wherever it happens
None — politics happens only in Parliament
Only the maintenance fee — money makes it political
None — politics means elections
discovery.answer: All of it — collective decision-making under scarcity with binding outcomes is politics, wherever it happens
discovery.hook: Even universal agreement wouldn't abolish politics — resources stay scarce and someone must still authoritatively allocate them.

c11_ps_ch01.mission: Test whether defining politics as 'everyday negotiation' drains the concept, and separate the analytic sense from the 'dirty politics' slur.
c11_ps_ch01.finale: Politics isn't what politicians do badly — it's what humans do whenever a shared decision must bind everyone.
c11_ps_ch01.subtitle: Find the politics in your dining table, not just in Delhi.
c11_ps_ch01.role: an analyst spotting collective decisions in disguise
c11_ps_ch01.intro: If politics were only elections and speeches, most of the decisions that shape your day would have no name — they do.
c11_ps_ch01.goal: Define politics as authoritative collective choice and distinguish analysis from abuse.

discovery.question: 'Freedom means doing whatever I want, whenever I want, with no one stopping me.' Is that the textbook's freedom?
options: No — that's license; freedom is a protected minimum area of non-interference that itself requires rules to defend
Yes — any constraint is unfreedom
Yes — laws and freedom can't coexist
No — freedom only means free speech
discovery.answer: No — that's license; freedom is a protected minimum area of non-interference that itself requires rules to defend
discovery.hook: Aung San Suu Kyi's 'freedom from fear' is positive liberty — an internal condition the mere absence of state interference can't supply; caste and poverty constrain without a policeman in sight.

c11_ps_ch02.mission: Place 'freedom from fear' on the negative/positive liberty map, then judge whether a state that simply stops interfering produces free people.
c11_ps_ch02.finale: Remove every law and the strong constrain the weak — a free society needs rules precisely so that interference has a border.
c11_ps_ch02.subtitle: Learn why a free person needs rules, not just an empty field.
c11_ps_ch02.role: a citizen measuring freedom by its protected core
c11_ps_ch02.intro: Absolute absence of constraint sounds like freedom — until you ask whose constraint disappears first, and whose arrives next.
c11_ps_ch02.goal: Distinguish negative and positive liberty and license from freedom.

discovery.question: Ramps for the disabled, maternity leave, reservations — differential treatment, therefore violations of equality?
options: No — treating unequals identically entrenches inequality; substantive equality demands treating different needs differently
Yes — equality means identical rules
Yes — but only reservations violate it
No — because these are all laws
discovery.answer: No — treating unequals identically entrenches inequality; substantive equality demands treating different needs differently
discovery.hook: And 'natural' inequality isn't a fixed excuse — technology keeps rewriting what biology means for life chances, as a screen reader or a Hawking's wheelchair shows.

c11_ps_ch03.mission: Sort entrenched inequalities from chosen ones, then judge whether a just society may leave economic outcomes entirely to the market.
c11_ps_ch03.finale: Equal protection and equal treatment aren't twins — a ramp breaks formal sameness to deliver actual equality.
c11_ps_ch03.subtitle: See why identical treatment can be the unfair one.
c11_ps_ch03.role: a policymaker choosing when sameness is injustice
c11_ps_ch03.intro: Same stairs for everyone is 'equal' — and the wheelchair user pays for it; equality has to look past the rule to the outcome.
c11_ps_ch03.goal: Distinguish formal from substantive equality and evaluate natural versus social inequality.

discovery.question: Free mid-day meals in government schools — charity or justice?
options: Justice — feeding a hungry child repairs a background inequality that rigged the classroom competition before it began
Charity — it goes beyond what anyone is owed
Charity — justice only covers courts
Neither — it's just a lunch scheme
discovery.answer: Justice — feeding a hungry child repairs a background inequality that rigged the classroom competition before it began
discovery.hook: The three principles of justice interlock rather than compete — equal basic rights, proportional rewards, and special treatment for disadvantaged needs all apply in different domains.

c11_ps_ch04.mission: Apply all three principles to one school — vote, prize and meal — then test Rawls' veil against the 'real people know who they are' objection.
c11_ps_ch04.finale: Behind the veil you don't know if you're the feeder or the fed — that's precisely what makes the chosen rule just rather than convenient.
c11_ps_ch04.subtitle: Ask whether a meal can be a right, not a favour.
c11_ps_ch04.role: a judge of rules chosen without knowing your own address
c11_ps_ch04.intro: Design society's rules before you know which family you're born into — Rawls' blindfold turns fairness into a thought experiment.
c11_ps_ch04.goal: Apply the three principles of justice and Rawls' original position to concrete policy.

discovery.question: Rights are gifts the government hands down to citizens — agree?
options: No — rights are claims society recognises as necessary for a life of dignity; the state enforces them, it doesn't bestow them
Yes — no law, no right
Yes — constitutions create rights from nothing
No — rights are natural like weather, needing no recognition
discovery.answer: No — rights are claims society recognises as necessary for a life of dignity; the state enforces them, it doesn't bestow them
discovery.hook: The right to privacy was morally real before Puttaswamy made it legally explicit — moral rights lead; legal rights follow and enforce.

c11_ps_ch05.mission: Filter 'right to bunk class' and 'right to clean water' through the dignity test, then weigh whether legal rights are superior merely because courts enforce them.
c11_ps_ch05.finale: A right that exists only on paper when courts close is weaker than a claim society has learned to defend — recognition is the substance, law the clothing.
c11_ps_ch05.subtitle: Discover why your rights predate the documents that list them.
c11_ps_ch05.role: a claimant arguing for a right that isn't written yet
c11_ps_ch05.intro: Majorities have demanded things that were never rights — the test isn't popularity, it's necessity for a dignified life.
c11_ps_ch05.goal: Define rights as recognised claims and weigh moral against legal rights.

discovery.question: Aadhaar card, voter ID, passport in hand — am I therefore a full citizen?
options: Only on paper — legal status is necessary but insufficient; rights aren't self-executing without citizens who monitor, demand and participate
Yes — documents are citizenship
Yes — the state will deliver the rest
No — documents prove nothing
discovery.answer: Only on paper — legal status is necessary but insufficient; rights aren't self-executing without citizens who monitor, demand and participate
discovery.hook: And 'equal citizenship' isn't identical treatment — different groups carry different needs, and uniform policy can be the unequal one.

c11_ps_ch06.mission: Run the free-rider test on a democracy where 90% merely vote and 10% do the watchdogging, then trace how movements made citizenship a project.
c11_ps_ch06.finale: Democratic citizenship is a project, not a possession — the Olga Tellis pavement-dwellers got heard because someone kept demanding.
c11_ps_ch06.subtitle: Learn why the ID card is the beginning of citizenship, not the end.
c11_ps_ch06.role: a citizen auditing whether status alone delivers rights
c11_ps_ch06.intro: You hold the right to clean water and a dusty ward office that never meets — between the document and the delivery sits participation.
c11_ps_ch06.goal: Separate legal status from active citizenship and evaluate the free-rider problem.

discovery.question: Benedict Anderson called the nation an 'imagined community' — so nations are fake?
options: No — 'imagined' means built through shared identification by people who'll never meet; constructed isn't fictional
Yes — imagination is fantasy
Yes — only shared blood makes a real nation
No — India is the exception that's real
discovery.answer: No — 'imagined' means built through shared identification by people who'll never meet; constructed isn't fictional
discovery.hook: And a nation isn't a state — India's nationhood doesn't need one language or one religion; the democratic claim is that political values, not cultural sameness, bind it.

c11_ps_ch07.mission: Test 'the Indian nation was born on 15 August 1947' against continuing historical identity, then assess whether shared political ideals can hold a multi-ethnic nation.
c11_ps_ch07.finale: Nationalism says nation and state should align; democracy replies that the alignment can be forged from constitutional commitment, not ancestry.
c11_ps_ch07.subtitle: Learn why 'imagined' communities are real — and nations needn't be uniform.
c11_ps_ch07.role: a theorist separating the nation from the state
c11_ps_ch07.intro: You've never met a hundred million fellow citizens, yet you share a nation with them — that act of imagination is the community.
c11_ps_ch07.goal: Distinguish nation from state and evaluate value-based versus culture-based nationalism.

discovery.question: Indian secularism: equal funding for all religions, or a wall that never touches religion at all?
options: Neither — it permits principled intervention (banning triple talaq, temple reform) to oppose domination while respecting faith
Equal support for every religion
Total separation — the state stays out entirely
Whatever the majority religion prefers
discovery.answer: Neither — it permits principled intervention (banning triple talaq, temple reform) to oppose domination while respecting faith
discovery.hook: Secularism isn't anti-religious — it fights domination inside and between religions, not the faith itself; intervention can serve values religion shares.

c11_ps_ch08.mission: Judge whether 'Sarva Dharma Samabhava' forbids the state from reforming a harmful practice, and contrast the Indian model with the American wall.
c11_ps_ch08.finale: Neutrality in India means even-handed pursuit of constitutional values — sometimes that requires stepping in, not staying out.
c11_ps_ch08.subtitle: Meet a secularism that intervenes — on principle.
c11_ps_ch08.role: a constitutional designer choosing between a wall and a scalpel
c11_ps_ch08.intro: A state that funds a madrasa and bans a discriminatory practice in the same year isn't confused — it's a different model of secular.
c11_ps_ch08.goal: Contrast Indian principled-distance secularism with strict separation and equal-respect readings.

discovery.question: A state reports zero riots and zero homicides for a decade — has it achieved peace?
options: Only negative peace — the absence of violence; structural injustice like unresolved water disputes can keep positive peace unmet
Yes — no violence means peace
Yes — law and order is peace
Only if the police agree
discovery.answer: Only negative peace — the absence of violence; structural injustice like unresolved water disputes can keep positive peace unmet
discovery.hook: 'Negative' isn't a moral grade — a ceasefire is negative peace and still essential; it just can't finish the job alone.

c11_ps_ch09.mission: Diagnose a calm Punjab as negative or positive peace, then name the structural blocks that keep ceasefires from becoming justice.
c11_ps_ch09.finale: Quiet streets can sit over loud grievances — positive peace is the presence of justice, not merely the absence of sirens.
c11_ps_ch09.subtitle: Tell the silence of peace from the silence of suppression.
c11_ps_ch09.role: a peace researcher reading past the crime statistics
c11_ps_ch09.intro: No riots reported — yet the river dispute festers and the prisoners wait. Something important is missing from the headline.
c11_ps_ch09.goal: Distinguish negative from positive peace and identify structural violence beneath calm.

discovery.question: Parliament can amend the Constitution under Article 368 — so Parliament, not the Constitution, is truly supreme?
options: No — the Basic Structure doctrine (Kesavananda 1973) means even amendments face constitutional limits; the text outranks its editors
Yes — whoever amends is sovereign
Yes — the UK model applies here
No — because the President can veto amendments
discovery.answer: No — the Basic Structure doctrine (Kesavananda 1973) means even amendments face constitutional limits; the text outranks its editors
discovery.hook: And the Court isn't above the Constitution either — constitutional supremacy means everyone, elected or appointed, answers to the document.

c11_ps_ch10.mission: Explain how unelected judges could strike down the NJAC Act without becoming supreme themselves, then argue whether virtuous leaders make constitutions unnecessary.
c11_ps_ch10.finale: A constitution isn't just a rights list — it's the machine that stops a well-meaning majority from easily unmaking them.
c11_ps_ch10.subtitle: Discover the document that binds even its own amenders.
c11_ps_ch10.role: a constitutional lawyer asking who guards the guardrails
c11_ps_ch10.intro: Parliament passed a law; the Court struck it down; neither is sovereign — in India the document itself sits at the top.
c11_ps_ch10.goal: Explain constitutional supremacy, the Basic Structure doctrine, and constitutionalism's logic.

discovery.question: They're called *fundamental* rights — so no government can restrict them, ever?
options: No — 'fundamental' isn't 'absolute': Article 19(2) alone lists eight grounds for reasonable restriction on free speech
Yes — fundamental means untouchable
Yes — that's what Part III guarantees
No — because rights were abolished in 1976
discovery.answer: No — 'fundamental' isn't 'absolute': Article 19(2) alone lists eight grounds for reasonable restriction on free speech
discovery.hook: And 'the State' reaches further than government offices — ONGC, SEBI and aided universities all count under Article 12, though the boundary is a test, not a title.

c11_ps_ch11.mission: Weigh the charge that unelected judges striking laws is anti-democratic, then judge whether Articles 33–34 hole the basic structure.
c11_ps_ch11.finale: Rights with no restriction clauses would collide with each other — the limits are how many rights can coexist at once.
c11_ps_ch11.subtitle: Learn why the strongest rights still carry asterisks.
c11_ps_ch11.role: a rights lawyer reading the fine print of Article 19
c11_ps_ch11.intro: The same Article that guarantees your speech lists eight ways it can be reasonably limited — the clause is the design, not the loophole.
c11_ps_ch11.goal: Apply restriction clauses to fundamental rights and define 'State' under Article 12.

discovery.question: The people are sovereign — so why can't citizens vote directly on the farm laws themselves?
options: Because Indian sovereignty is exercised through representatives — the people authorise power but don't wield it law-by-law
Because the Constitution forgot referendums
Because voters aren't educated enough
No reason — direct voting is actually allowed
discovery.answer: Because Indian sovereignty is exercised through representatives — the people authorise power but don't wield it law-by-law
discovery.hook: And the President isn't picked by the PM — an electoral college of elected MPs and MLAs votes; indirect election means representatives choose, not the executive.

c11_ps_ch12.mission: Weigh simultaneous elections against accountability, then argue two points each for and against a directly elected President.
c11_ps_ch12.finale: Representation means the people hand out power and call it back — sovereignty lives in the authorisation, not in a daily referendum.
c11_ps_ch12.subtitle: See why your vote is sovereignty delegated, not sovereignty diluted.
c11_ps_ch12.role: a voter tracing where their ballot's power actually travels
c11_ps_ch12.intro: You never vote on a single law — yet you're still sovereign; the difference between authorising and exercising is the system.
c11_ps_ch12.goal: Distinguish popular sovereignty from direct rule and explain indirect election mechanics.

discovery.question: Who actually implements the Right to Education Act in a district — the Education Minister?
options: The permanent executive — District Education Officers, block officers, inspectors; the bureaucracy is an integral tier of the executive, not its servant
The Education Minister alone
The Lok Sabha's education committee
The President's secretariat
discovery.answer: The permanent executive — District Education Officers, block officers, inspectors; the bureaucracy is an integral tier of the executive, not its servant
discovery.hook: And parliamentary doesn't mean 'no separation' — ministers are MPs (fused personnel) but the functions stay distinct; presidential systems do the reverse.

c11_ps_ch13.mission: Map political versus permanent executive on one Act's journey to a classroom, then test whether fixed-term presidentialism beats India's coalition instability.
c11_ps_ch13.finale: Ministers answer to the Lok Sabha collectively — yet the same majority that sustains them is the leash that holds them.
c11_ps_ch13.subtitle: Meet the executive that outlasts every minister.
c11_ps_ch13.role: a tracer following a law from cabinet to classroom
c11_ps_ch13.intro: The minister signs the policy; a thousand permanent officers make it real — both are 'the executive.'
c11_ps_ch13.goal: Distinguish political and permanent executive and compare parliamentary with presidential design.

discovery.question: The executive commands a majority inside the legislature — so parliamentary oversight is basically a myth?
options: No — Question Hour, no-confidence motions, committees and sole control of Money Bills give the House real teeth
Yes — the majority makes scrutiny theatre
Yes — the Cabinet decides everything
No — only because of the Opposition
discovery.answer: No — Question Hour, no-confidence motions, committees and sole control of Money Bills give the House real teeth
discovery.hook: The Rajya Sabha isn't a weaker Lok Sabha — it matches it on amendments, ordinary bills and impeachment; only money and confidence tilt to the lower House.

c11_ps_ch14.mission: Track how a passed law can still be repealed under pressure (the farm laws), then defend whether an indirectly elected upper House is 'undemocratic obstruction.'
c11_ps_ch14.finale: The executive proposes, but the legislature's power to reject, amend, interrogate and defund is what makes proposing meaningful.
c11_ps_ch14.subtitle: See the legislature's real job: not passing laws but holding power.
c11_ps_ch14.role: an MP choosing between whip and question hour
c11_ps_ch14.intro: A government with a brute majority still must face Question Hour every morning — accountability survives even when votes don't.
c11_ps_ch14.goal: Evaluate legislative oversight tools and the Rajya Sabha's federal role.

discovery.question: Judicial independence means judges can decide cases however they like, accountable to no one — right?
options: No — independence insulates courts from political control; accountability still runs through impeachment, appeals and reasoned public judgments
Yes — that's what independence means
Yes — judges are above the law
No — judges answer to the executive
discovery.answer: No — independence insulates courts from political control; accountability still runs through impeachment, appeals and reasoned public judgments
discovery.hook: The collegium isn't in the Constitution's text — the word is 'consultation,' read as 'concurrence' by the Three Judges Cases; the system was built by interpretation, not drafting.

c11_ps_ch15.mission: Trace how 'consultation' became 'concurrence,' then weigh whether a self-appointing judiciary breaks checks and balances.
c11_ps_ch15.finale: Insulation isn't licence — the judge who can't be pressured also can't be arbitrary, because every judgment must argue itself in public.
c11_ps_ch15.subtitle: Distinguish a court shielded from politics from a court above the law.
c11_ps_ch15.role: a jurist defending independence without claiming impunity
c11_ps_ch15.intro: A court that can strike down a cabinet's law must be unfrightened — but unfrightened is not the same as unaccountable.
c11_ps_ch15.goal: Explain judicial independence's limits and the collegium's interpretive origin.

discovery.question: President's Rule, national emergency, financial emergency — do these convert India into a unitary state for good?
options: Temporarily and reversibly — the Union gains power during the emergency, but safeguards and expiry return the federal structure
Yes — emergencies make India unitary permanently
Yes — Article 356 is the rule, not the exception
No — emergencies don't change anything
discovery.answer: Temporarily and reversibly — the Union gains power during the emergency, but safeguards and expiry return the federal structure
discovery.hook: And the Concurrent List isn't 'shared administration' — it's shared legislative competence; both may legislate, Union law prevails on clash, which is cooperation, not encroachment.

c11_ps_ch16.mission: List India's asymmetric features — residuary powers, State reorganisation, emergency control — then defend the Concurrent List as cooperative design.
c11_ps_ch16.finale: A federation that can flex in crisis and spring back after is asymmetrical by design — the unitary moment has an off switch.
c11_ps_ch16.subtitle: Read federalism that bends in emergencies without breaking.
c11_ps_ch16.role: a federal analyst weighing shared lists and emergency clauses
c11_ps_ch16.intro: A unitary system can have strong local bodies and a federal one can go unitary in crisis — labels lie; check where the power is anchored.
c11_ps_ch16.goal: Characterise Indian federalism's asymmetry and evaluate emergency conversion.

discovery.question: The 73rd and 74th Amendments of 1992 created Panchayati Raj — true?
options: No — statutory panchayats existed since the 1950s; the amendments made them a constitutional entitlement states could no longer suspend or starve
Yes — before 1992 there were no panchayats
Yes — the amendments invented local government
No — panchayats began in 1947
discovery.answer: No — statutory panchayats existed since the 1950s; the amendments made them a constitutional entitlement states could no longer suspend or starve
discovery.hook: The real change: Bihar went without panchayat elections for years pre-1992; after the amendments, elections, a state election commission and finance commission became mandatory.

c11_ps_ch17.mission: Compare a dissolvable pre-1992 body with a constitutionally protected one, then argue why 'states administer better by scale' misses the point.
c11_ps_ch17.finale: Local government isn't an efficiency scheme — it's the third tier of democracy, and the amendments made it unfireable.
c11_ps_ch17.subtitle: Discover what changed in 1992 — not the panchayat, but its permanence.
c11_ps_ch17.role: a district planner distinguishing agency from tier of government
c11_ps_ch17.intro: Same village council, new status — before 1992 a state could dissolve it at will; after, the Constitution itself guaranteed the chair.
c11_ps_ch17.goal: Explain the 73rd/74th Amendments' constitutionalisation of local government.

discovery.question: 105+ amendments in 74 years — proof the Indian Constitution was defective from the start?
options: No — most changes were technical or simple-majority; the core held, and the Court struck the few amendments that attacked it
Yes — good constitutions never need amending
Yes — each amendment shows a design failure
No — because all 105 were ceremonial
discovery.answer: No — most changes were technical or simple-majority; the core held, and the Court struck the few amendments that attacked it
discovery.hook: 'Living document' doesn't mean infinitely malleable — the 42nd Amendment learned that when its key provisions were struck down; the document grows within a core.

c11_ps_ch18.mission: Sort which changes need Article 368's special majority (and which don't), then judge whether state ratification makes the system undemocratically rigid.
c11_ps_ch18.finale: Adaptability is the feature — a constitution that couldn't bend would have broken; the ones that survive are the ones allowed to grow.
c11_ps_ch18.subtitle: Learn how a document can be living without being liquid.
c11_ps_ch18.role: a constitutional historian counting amendments honestly
c11_ps_ch18.intro: A constitution amended over a hundred times that still reads like itself — the changes are the maintenance, not the malfunction.
c11_ps_ch18.goal: Evaluate amendment frequency versus stability and the layers of amendment procedure.

discovery.question: The 'sociological imagination' means feeling what a homeless person feels — empathy, upgraded?
options: No — Mills meant structural mapping: tracing how housing policy, land markets and migration produce the homelessness, not feeling it
Yes — imagination is empathy
Yes — anyone who reads the news has it
No — it's just Berger being poetic about spying
discovery.answer: No — Mills meant structural mapping: tracing how housing policy, land markets and migration produce the homelessness, not feeling it
discovery.hook: And 'dialectical' isn't a fight between individual and society — each constitutes the other; society exists through people, people become social through it.

c11_soc_ch01.mission: Apply the imagination to a housing scheme: does gifting houses close a public issue, or leave the structure that produces it untouched?
c11_soc_ch01.finale: The sociologist is a spy among the familiar — the everyday street looks different once you see the structures standing behind it.
c11_soc_ch01.subtitle: Trade empathy for structure — and see biography meet history.
c11_soc_ch01.role: a sociologist mapping the invisible wiring under everyday life
c11_soc_ch01.intro: The news reader sees a person without a house; the sociological imagination sees the markets and policies that built the homelessness.
c11_soc_ch01.goal: Define the sociological imagination and the individual–society dialectic.

discovery.question: Teenagers share an age and a world of problems — so they're a social group?
options: No — it's a statistical category; a group needs interaction, roles and a sense of 'we', not just a common label
Yes — a shared label makes a group
Yes — they're even a primary group
No — only families count as groups
discovery.answer: No — it's a statistical category; a group needs interaction, roles and a sense of 'we', not just a common label
discovery.hook: A status outlives its holder — the principal's chair carries rights and duties no matter who sits in it; the concept is a slot, not a person.

c11_soc_ch02.mission: Separate quasi-groups from real ones, then test whether contested concepts like 'caste' are too unstable for scientific study.
c11_soc_ch02.finale: A status is a position with normative rights and duties; the person occupying it is replaceable — that's what makes it structural.
c11_soc_ch02.subtitle: Learn why a shared label is not a shared life.
c11_soc_ch02.role: a sociologist auditing which collections deserve the name 'group'
c11_soc_ch02.intro: A thousand strangers share the label 'Delhiite' — they also share nothing else; the group begins where interaction begins.
c11_soc_ch02.goal: Distinguish social groups from categories and use status, role and institution precisely.

discovery.question: Industrialisation marches in, and the nuclear family inevitably replaces the joint family — a law of modernisation?
options: No — Shah's evidence showed joint families grew with post-independence life expectancy; 'broken' and 'modern' family stories don't fit India
Yes — cities atomise kin
Yes — joint families are a relic
No — joint families never existed anyway
discovery.answer: No — Shah's evidence showed joint families grew with post-independence life expectancy; 'broken' and 'modern' family stories don't fit India
discovery.hook: And your school isn't the institution — education is; the school is an organisation that embodies it, which is why a principal can change rules but not 'the institution.'

c11_soc_ch03.mission: Correct 'school = institution' into 'school = organisation,' then weigh functionalist versus conflict readings of one institution.
c11_soc_ch03.finale: Institutions are patterns, not buildings — education persists while every school in it reorganises.
c11_soc_ch03.subtitle: Tell the building from the institution — and the data from the modernisation myth.
c11_soc_ch03.role: a sociologist refusing to call a building a pattern
c11_soc_ch03.intro: The principal changed the rules; the institution didn't blink — institutions are the pattern, organisations merely their local costumes.
c11_soc_ch03.goal: Distinguish institutions from organisations and apply empirical checks to family-change theory.

discovery.question: 'Cultured' people attend classical concerts — so culture means refined art and literature?
options: No — Tylor's shift was from elite art to the whole way of life; your lunch, slang and seating habits are culture too
Yes — culture is high art
Yes — the rest is just habit
No — because culture only means tradition
discovery.answer: No — Tylor's shift was from elite art to the whole way of life; your lunch, slang and seating habits are culture too
discovery.hook: And material culture outruns non-material — the smartphone arrived faster than the norms for it; that gap is culture lag, not chaos.

c11_soc_ch04.mission: Split one temple into its material, cognitive and normative layers at once, then weigh whether Geertz's meanings make Tylor obsolete.
c11_soc_ch04.finale: A temple is stone (material), cosmology (cognitive) and rules of entry (normative) in one object — the dimensions are lenses, not compartments.
c11_soc_ch04.subtitle: Discover that your lunch is as much culture as a raga.
c11_soc_ch04.role: an anthropologist reading a whole way of life
c11_soc_ch04.intro: Culture isn't the concert hall — it's also the queue outside it, the ticket app, and who sits where inside.
c11_soc_ch04.goal: Define culture as a whole way of life and apply its three simultaneous dimensions.

discovery.question: Complete objectivity is impossible in sociology — so all research is just the researcher's opinion?
options: No — objectivity is an ongoing process of documenting methods and practising self-reflexivity; impossible-to-perfect isn't permission to stop
Yes — abandon the pretence
Yes — every study is equal
No — sociologists must become machines
discovery.answer: No — objectivity is an ongoing process of documenting methods and practising self-reflexivity; impossible-to-perfect isn't permission to stop
discovery.hook: Subjectivity isn't bias you can suppress — it's your caste, class and gender shaping what you notice; naming it is the method, not the failure.

c11_soc_ch05.mission: Separate method from methodology, then grade a study by whether it disclosed its lens rather than whether it claimed to have none.
c11_soc_ch05.finale: The honest researcher doesn't claim to be neutral — they show you where they stood, so you can judge what they saw.
c11_soc_ch05.subtitle: Learn that confessing your lens is more objective than denying it.
c11_soc_ch05.role: a fieldworker auditing their own blind spots
c11_soc_ch05.intro: Where you stand decides what you see — sociology's answer isn't pretending to float, it's reporting the ground underfoot.
c11_soc_ch05.goal: Distinguish method from methodology and apply reflexivity as a rigour practice.

discovery.question: Fix poverty and caste and gender inequality will fade automatically — is stratification really just economics?
options: No — stratification runs on several axes at once; gender cuts across every caste and class, so money alone can't level it
Yes — class is the master key
Yes — poverty causes all hierarchy
No — because caste no longer exists
discovery.answer: No — stratification runs on several axes at once; gender cuts across every caste and class, so money alone can't level it
discovery.hook: And 'competition is human nature' is a naturalistic fallacy — cooperation and competition are both socially organised; no society runs on instinct.

c11_soc_ch06.mission: Draw a school's structure as statuses and roles (not rules), then test whether 'socialism failed because it fought human nature' survives sociology.
c11_soc_ch06.finale: Structure isn't the rulebook — it's the arrangement of positions that the rules merely serve.
c11_soc_ch06.subtitle: See hierarchy as many ladders crossing, not one economic ladder.
c11_soc_ch06.role: a sociologist redrawing a school as positions, not rules
c11_soc_ch06.intro: Uniform codes aren't the school's structure — student, teacher, principal and the expectations between them are.
c11_soc_ch06.goal: Define social structure relationally and stratification as multi-dimensional.

discovery.question: Smartphones, new slang, a viral fashion — is that 'social change'?
options: Not yet — social change means structural transformation at scale; gadgets only count once they reorganise family, work or polity
Yes — any visible difference is social change
Yes — slang is society changing
Not yet — only revolutions count
discovery.answer: Not yet — social change means structural transformation at scale; gadgets only count once they reorganise family, work or polity
discovery.hook: And 'revolutionary' doesn't mean 'structural' alone — the Green Revolution was both fast AND structural, while slow English-education reform quietly built universities and a civil service.

c11_soc_ch07.mission: Classify the Green Revolution and the Bengal Renaissance by pace AND depth together, then check whether sociology arose only because Europe 'changed faster.'
c11_soc_ch07.finale: Change becomes social change when it moves the furniture of institutions — not when it merely changes the wallpaper.
c11_soc_ch07.subtitle: Learn the difference between a fad and a restructuring.
c11_soc_ch07.role: a change-tracker separating surface churn from deep shifts
c11_soc_ch07.intro: A new app is noise; a new institution is change — the test is whether the underlying structure had to move.
c11_soc_ch07.goal: Distinguish structural from surface change and classify by pace and nature together.

discovery.question: Climate change is a purely natural phenomenon — human society isn't meaningfully implicated. Sound?
options: No — the relation is a feedback loop: society reshapes ecology, and the altered ecology then reshapes society
Yes — nature runs on its own
Yes — humans are too small to matter
No — because ecology stops where cities begin
discovery.answer: No — the relation is a feedback loop: society reshapes ecology, and the altered ecology then reshapes society
discovery.hook: Even the 'pristine' is manufactured — Delhi's Ridge and Corbett's meadows are products of past human intervention wearing a natural costume.

c11_soc_ch08.mission: Trace one deforestation loop — society to soil erosion to forced migration back into society — then judge whether better tech alone can manage the environment.
c11_soc_ch08.finale: Humans aren't nature's visitors — we're inside the ecology we keep editing, and the edits answer back.
c11_soc_ch08.subtitle: Follow the arrow that bends back on itself.
c11_soc_ch08.role: an environmental sociologist tracing a two-way street
c11_soc_ch08.intro: The 'untouched wilderness' was often someone's farm or forest management once — society and ecology have been co-authoring all along.
c11_soc_ch08.goal: Model the society–environment relationship as dialectical, not one-directional.

discovery.question: Sociology was born because Enlightenment, then Revolution, then Industry happened in sequence — a tidy timeline?
options: It's a triad, not a timeline — Enlightenment gave the method, the French Revolution the subject, the Industrial Revolution the object
Yes — history happened first, sociology after
Yes — Europe changed faster, so sociology started there
No — it was invented by one founder
discovery.answer: It's a triad, not a timeline — Enlightenment gave the method, the French Revolution the subject, the Industrial Revolution the object
discovery.hook: Marx's exile wasn't biography trivia — the British Museum Reading Room's factory reports and Hansard debates are the empirical spine of Capital.

c11_soc_ch09.mission: Match each revolution to its epistemic gift, then argue whether the Manifesto is a pamphlet for history or a text for sociology.
c11_soc_ch09.finale: The modern state needed to govern health, crime and 'development' — and that demand for new knowledge is where sociology came from.
c11_soc_ch09.subtitle: See three revolutions as one engine with three parts.
c11_soc_ch09.role: a historian of ideas assembling sociology's engine
c11_soc_ch09.intro: Reason as method, the sovereign individual as subject, industrial pathology as object — three gifts, one discipline.
c11_soc_ch09.goal: Explain sociology's birth through the method–subject–object triad and state demand for knowledge.

discovery.question: Sociology and social anthropology merged in Indian universities because the theories had converged — an intellectual marriage?
options: Mostly an administrative compromise — resource scarcity and colonial funding structures forced the departments together
Yes — the theories naturally united
Yes — Ghurye designed it as theory
No — they never actually merged
discovery.answer: Mostly an administrative compromise — resource scarcity and colonial funding structures forced the departments together
discovery.hook: The discipline was built by improvisation: Ghurye's 35-year headship controlled appointments and journals; Calcutta's anthropology existed because the colonial state needed ethnographic surveys.

c11_soc_ch10.mission: Weigh A.R. Desai's Marxist lens against Ghurye's diffusionism for reading post-independence India — using the three dilemmas the colonial context created.
c11_soc_ch10.finale: Colonialism wasn't just the villain — it set the questions: what is a colony's sociology for, and who is the anthropologist's 'primitive' inside a civilisation?
c11_soc_ch10.subtitle: Discover the discipline built by necessity, not just by ideas.
c11_soc_ch10.role: an archivist of how Indian sociology was actually assembled
c11_soc_ch10.intro: Great thinkers get the credit — but syllabi, journals and colonial survey budgets did the building.
c11_soc_ch10.goal: Explain how institutions and the colonial context shaped Indian sociology's questions.

discovery.question: 'Gender' and 'skill level' can't be statistics — the subject only deals in numbers. True?
options: No — statistics handles qualitative data too; it classifies and counts attributes just as it measures quantities
Yes — no numbers, no statistics
Yes — but only at Class 11 level
No — because gender can be coded as numbers
discovery.answer: No — statistics handles qualitative data too; it classifies and counts attributes just as it measures quantities
discovery.hook: 'Statistics' in the singular isn't a single number — it's the science of collecting, analysing and interpreting data; the plural is the data itself.

c11_stat_ch01.mission: Separate singular from plural senses, then judge whether unpredictable human behaviour makes statistical forecasting of GDP useless.
c11_stat_ch01.finale: Economics without statistics is intuition; governments plan crops, budgets and inflation targets on the forecasts intuition can't give.
c11_stat_ch01.subtitle: Learn that the word 'statistics' carries two meanings — and qualitative counts.
c11_stat_ch01.role: a statistician defending the subject's borders
c11_stat_ch01.intro: Is 'statistics' a number or a science? The answer decides what the subject is even allowed to study.
c11_stat_ch01.goal: Distinguish singular/plural statistics and qualitative from quantitative data.

discovery.question: Secondary data is just a fallback — always collect primary data when you can. Sound policy?
options: No — secondary data often wins on cost, time and coverage; the research objective, not the data's origin, chooses the method
Yes — firsthand is always best
Yes — old data is useless
No — secondary data is always better
discovery.answer: No — secondary data often wins on cost, time and coverage; the research objective, not the data's origin, chooses the method
discovery.hook: Handing someone a questionnaire isn't 'direct personal investigation' — in DPI the investigator asks aloud and records; the respondent never writes.

c11_stat_ch02.mission: Pick the right collection method for a tight budget and a dispersed population, then argue three cases where DPI fails to be 'the best.'
c11_stat_ch02.finale: Primary data answers your exact question at a price; secondary data answers nearly your question for free — choose by objective.
c11_stat_ch02.subtitle: Learn when yesterday's data beats today's survey.
c11_stat_ch02.role: a researcher matching method to question, budget and clock
c11_stat_ch02.intro: The census exists — yet students still want to knock on a crore doors; knowing when existing data suffices is the skill.
c11_stat_ch02.goal: Choose between primary and secondary data and apply the direct investigation method correctly.

discovery.question: 500 families, number of children each ranging 0–8 — build a frequency distribution with class intervals?
options: No — a discrete variable with a tiny range wants a frequency array; grouping 0–8 into classes destroys information
Yes — all quantitative data needs classes
Yes — 0-2, 3-5, 6-8 will do
No — because families aren't data
discovery.answer: No — a discrete variable with a tiny range wants a frequency array; grouping 0–8 into classes destroys information
discovery.hook: Classification is the decision, the frequency table merely its output — choosing 'by state' versus 'by year' versus 'by size' is the actual analysis.

c11_stat_ch03.mission: Classify the same literacy data four ways — chronological, geographical, qualitative, quantitative — then defend why chronology beats labels for a GDP trend.
c11_stat_ch03.finale: A frequency table isn't classification — it's what classification looks like once you've decided what to group by.
c11_stat_ch03.subtitle: Learn that grouping is a choice, not a format.
c11_stat_ch03.role: a data organiser deciding what the columns should mean
c11_stat_ch03.intro: The kabadiwallah sorting junk is classifying; the count per pile is just the receipt — decide the criterion first.
c11_stat_ch03.goal: Distinguish classification bases and choose array versus distribution correctly.

discovery.question: A farmers' income table has intervals and frequencies but no Note — is the omission harmless?
options: No — without a note the reader can't tell if the last open class (500000+) was handled, or the data's source and units; the note is part of the table
Yes — notes are decoration
Yes — titles cover everything
No — because tables must have footnotes legally
discovery.answer: No — without a note the reader can't tell if the last open class (500000+) was handled, or the data's source and units; the note is part of the table
discovery.hook: And stubs and captions aren't fixed positions — put whichever comparison matters where the eye can compare it; layout serves the reader, not the rule.

c11_stat_ch04.mission: Present 102 crore of census data in text and feel its limits, then choose stubs versus captions for rainfall across 12 months and 5 cities.
c11_stat_ch04.finale: Text can carry exact numbers — but the moment readers must compare, the table earns its grid.
c11_stat_ch04.subtitle: Decide when prose holds numbers and when only a table will do.
c11_stat_ch04.role: a presenter choosing between a paragraph and a grid
c11_stat_ch04.intro: A sentence can say '53 crore males' precisely — but five cities and twelve months of rain won't fit in prose.
c11_stat_ch04.goal: Apply textual and tabular presentation appropriately and structure tables correctly.

discovery.question: Data: 5, 7, 7, 8, 100. The 'average' is 25.4 — a fair summary?
options: No — one outlier dragged the mean past every real value; the median or mode, 7, represents the data honestly
Yes — mean is the average, end of story
Yes — 25.4 is mathematically correct
No — the true average is 8
discovery.answer: No — one outlier dragged the mean past every real value; the median or mode, 7, represents the data honestly
discovery.hook: And the assumed mean needn't be in the data — A is just a convenient origin; A = 16.5 gives the same mean as A = 15.

c11_stat_ch05.mission: Compare two localities' incomes where equal means hide opposite distributions, then compute a mean by the assumed-mean shortcut.
c11_stat_ch05.finale: An average is a spokesman, not a summary — ask whether it's representing the data or just describing it.
c11_stat_ch05.subtitle: Catch the outlier that hijacks the mean.
c11_stat_ch05.role: an analyst choosing which average deserves the headline
c11_stat_ch05.intro: Five numbers, one bully: the hundred pulls the mean off the page while the median calmly reports the middle.
c11_stat_ch05.goal: Choose between mean, median and mode by data shape and compute the assumed-mean method.

discovery.question: Districts A and B both average ₹50,000 household income — equal claims on the development fund?
options: No — B's ultra-rich few may hide mass poverty that A lacks; identical means with different dispersion are different realities
Yes — same mean, same need
Yes — allocation should follow averages
No — B should get less because it's richer
discovery.answer: No — B's ultra-rich few may hide mass poverty that A lacks; identical means with different dispersion are different realities
discovery.hook: And dividing any absolute measure by the mean doesn't make it a CV — the coefficient of variation is specifically σ/mean; the rest have their own names.

c11_stat_ch06.mission: Show how two investments can share a 12% average return with wildly different risk, then judge when CV itself misleads.
c11_stat_ch06.finale: The mean tells you the centre; dispersion tells you how much to trust it — a policy built on the first alone is half-blind.
c11_stat_ch06.subtitle: Learn why identical averages can describe opposite worlds.
c11_stat_ch06.role: a fund allocator looking past the average
c11_stat_ch06.intro: Same average income, opposite district — one evenly middle, one feast-and-famine; only dispersion sees the difference.
c11_stat_ch06.goal: Use dispersion measures to expose what central tendency hides.

discovery.question: Districts with more hospitals report more disease — therefore hospitals cause disease. Where's the fallacy?
options: A third variable — population density and urbanisation drive both; correlation measures co-movement, not causation
Nowhere — the correlation proves it
The hospitals were built badly
Correlation only works one way
discovery.answer: A third variable — population density and urbanisation drive both; correlation measures co-movement, not causation
discovery.hook: And r = 0.92 says 'strong and positive' but not automatically 'linear' — the coefficient can't see the curve your scatter diagram can.

c11_stat_ch07.mission: Explain how shoe size correlates with reading skill in children (the hidden variable: age), then test what r alone can and cannot claim.
c11_stat_ch07.finale: Correlation hears two things move together — it never hears which one is talking, or whether a third is conducting.
c11_stat_ch07.subtitle: Separate moving together from making happen.
c11_stat_ch07.role: a sceptic interrogating a suspicious correlation
c11_stat_ch07.intro: Bigger feet, better readers — the correlation is real, the causation is an illusion called age.
c11_stat_ch07.goal: Distinguish correlation from causation and read r's limits correctly.

discovery.question: WPI covers far more commodities than CPI — so it's the better inflation measure for the common man?
options: No — coverage isn't relevance; the common man buys the consumer basket, which is exactly what CPI tracks
Yes — more commodities means better
Yes — wholesale is the real economy
No — CPI covers more items actually
discovery.answer: No — coverage isn't relevance; the common man buys the consumer basket, which is exactly what CPI tracks
